quizzes.answer: Multiplying many small probabilities underflows numerically; summing their logs is numerically stable and gives the same maximizing parameter, since log is monotonic

quizzes.answer: Three times, because a lazy plan is re-executed from source on every action unless you cache it

quizzes.question: Why does Spark delay execution until an action is called?
quizzes.answer: To build an optimized execution plan across all operations

quizzes.answer: The shuffle — matching keys must be moved onto the same machine, which means sending data across the network

quizzes.question: You want each row alongside its group's average, keeping every original row. Does a groupBy do that?
quizzes.answer: No — grouping collapses each group to one row, so you need a window function to keep the rows and add the aggregate

quizzes.question: You want to find all students who have NO enrollments. Which join type gives you this result?

quizzes.question: You cache every intermediate DataFrame in your pipeline, just to be safe. What goes wrong?
quizzes.answer: Memory fills with results used once, which evicts the ones that are genuinely reused and can push work to disk

quizzes.question: You join a billion-row table against a two-hundred-row lookup table. Does that need a full shuffle?
quizzes.answer: No — the small table can be broadcast to every machine, so the large one never moves

quizzes.question: A DataFrame is the result of an expensive 5-table join. You need to run 4 different aggregations on it. What should you do?
quizzes.answer: Cache the DataFrame after the join, run all 4 aggregations, then unpersist — the join executes once, all aggregations read from cache

quizzes.question: Which of the three ETL stages is responsible for ensuring data conforms to the target schema — renaming columns, casting types, and normalising formats?
quizzes.answer: Transform — raw data is reshaped and cleaned into the target structure

quizzes.question: A dataset of 10 million rows is partitioned across 200 executors. How many rows does each executor process on average?
quizzes.answer: 50,000 rows

quizzes.question: Which of the following are true about Spark's lazy evaluation model? (Select all that apply)
quizzes.answer: Transformations such as filter() and map() are not executed when called — they build a DAG; An action such as collect() or count() triggers execution of the full lineage; Lazy evaluation allows Spark to optimise and combine multiple operations before running

quizzes.question: What does the following PySpark code return?\n\ndf.groupBy('city').agg({'revenue': 'sum', 'orders': 'count'}).orderBy('sum(revenue)', ascending=False)
quizzes.answer: A DataFrame with one row per city, showing total revenue and order count, sorted from highest to lowest revenue

quizzes.question: Which statements correctly describe the difference between PySpark DataFrames and Pandas DataFrames? (Select all that apply)
quizzes.answer: PySpark DataFrames are distributed across a cluster; Pandas DataFrames live in a single machine's memory; PySpark enforces a schema at the column level; Pandas infers types but does not enforce them; Calling toPandas() on a PySpark DataFrame collects all data to the driver node; PySpark show() prints the first n rows without collecting the full DataFrame to the driver

quizzes.question: Which PySpark method registers a DataFrame as a temporary SQL view so that spark.sql() can query it by name?
quizzes.answer: df.createOrReplaceTempView("view_name")

quizzes.question: What are the performance costs of using a PySpark UDF instead of a built-in function? (Select all that apply)
quizzes.answer: UDFs are executed row-by-row in Python, bypassing Spark's JVM-level optimiser (Catalyst); Each row must be serialised from JVM memory, passed to a Python process, and deserialised back; Spark cannot push predicates through a UDF, preventing filter push-down optimisations

quizzes.question: A data engineer runs df.dropDuplicates(['order_id', 'timestamp']) and then df.fillna({'discount': 0.0}). What is wrong with this sequence if the goal is to clean the data before analysis?
quizzes.answer: dropDuplicates() with a subset of columns will silently drop rows that have the same order_id and timestamp but different values in other columns — this may be intentional but should be verified

quizzes.question: Which PySpark function is used to break a column containing an array (e.g. a list of product tags) into one row per array element?
quizzes.answer: explode()

quizzes.question: Which of the following are valid reasons to use .cache() on a PySpark DataFrame? (Select all that apply)
quizzes.answer: The same DataFrame is the input for three separate downstream aggregations; An iterative machine-learning algorithm reads the training DataFrame on each epoch; An expensive joined and cleaned DataFrame will be reused by several actions

quizzes.question: What is the key reason a broadcast join is faster than a default sort-merge join when one table is small?
quizzes.answer: The small table is sent to every worker node so each partition of the large table can do a local lookup with no network shuffle

quizzes.question: A data exploration step runs df.describe() on a PySpark DataFrame. Which statistics does describe() compute for numeric columns?
quizzes.answer: count, mean, stddev, min, max

quizzes.question: Which of the following correctly describe how .persist() differs from .cache() in PySpark? (Select all that apply)
quizzes.answer: For DataFrames in Spark 3.0 and later, cache() uses MEMORY_AND_DISK_DESER by default; persist() accepts a StorageLevel argument such as MEMORY_AND_DISK or DISK_ONLY; With MEMORY_AND_DISK, partitions that do not fit in memory spill to disk instead of being recomputed

quizzes.question: You fit a straight line through data whose true relationship is a gentle curve. The fit still produces coefficients and an R-squared. What tells you something is wrong?
quizzes.answer: The residuals: they stop looking like noise and take on a visible curved pattern

quizzes.question: A house-price model gives a coefficient of 150 for square feet and 20,000 for bedrooms. Does that mean bedrooms matter more than floor area?
quizzes.answer: No — the two are measured in different units, so their raw sizes are not comparable

quizzes.question: You add a random column and refit unregularized OLS with an intercept on exactly the same training rows. What happens to training R-squared?
quizzes.answer: It rises, or at worst stays the same — R-squared never decreases when you add a predictor

quizzes.question: What does the Adjusted R-squared penalize compared to regular R-squared?
quizzes.answer: Adding more predictors to the model

headings.text: Interactive: Gradient Descent on Loss Landscape

quizzes.question: Ordinary least squares squares the residuals before adding them. Absolute values would also make them positive. Why square?
quizzes.answer: Squaring makes the cost a smooth convex bowl with an exact closed-form minimum, and it is what Gaussian noise implies

quizzes.question: The closed-form solution needs the inverse of X-transpose-X. Two of your feature columns are perfectly correlated. What happens?
quizzes.answer: The matrix is singular, so no inverse exists and there is no unique solution at all

quizzes.question: There is an exact formula for the best coefficients. So why would anyone use gradient descent for linear regression at all?
quizzes.answer: Because the formula inverts a matrix whose size grows with the number of features, which becomes impossible at scale

quizzes.question: In the Normal Equation, what condition is required for (X^T X)^{-1} to exist?
quizzes.answer: X must have full column rank (no perfect multicollinearity)

headings.text: Why Linear Regression Fails for Classification

quizzes.question: You fit an ordinary straight-line regression to labels that are only ever 0 or 1, then read the output as a probability. What can go wrong with the very first prediction?
quizzes.answer: It can come out negative or above 1, and no probability can be either

quizzes.question: We need a function that turns any real number into something between 0 and 1, never quite reaching either end, and rises smoothly throughout. Roughly what shape must its graph have?
quizzes.answer: An S-curve, flat at both ends and steepest in the middle

quizzes.question: A coefficient of 1.2 sits on family history in a diabetes model. Does that mean having a family history adds 1.2 to the probability of diabetes?
quizzes.answer: No — it adds 1.2 to the log-odds, which multiplies the odds by e to the 1.2, roughly a factor of 3.3

quizzes.question: A cancer screening model has Precision=0.60 and Recall=0.95. A fraud detection model has Precision=0.90 and Recall=0.55. Which metric is each model optimizing for, and which threshold setting achieves it?
quizzes.answer: Cancer model has low threshold (catching most positives at expense of false alarms); fraud model has high threshold (avoiding false alarms at expense of missing some fraud)

headings.text: Why Sigmoid? From Bernoulli to Logistic
Connecting the Mathematics: Linear vs. Logistic

quizzes.question: Many functions squash a real number into the range 0 to 1 — the sigmoid, the normal distribution's cumulative curve, and others. Was the sigmoid picked for logistic regression because it is convenient, or does something select it?
quizzes.answer: It falls out of writing the Bernoulli distribution in exponential-family form and setting its natural parameter equal to the linear predictor

quizzes.question: Linear regression has an exact formula for its best coefficients. Does logistic regression have one too?
quizzes.answer: No — the likelihood equations have no closed-form solution, so it must be solved iteratively

quizzes.question: You could train a classifier by squaring the difference between the predicted probability and the 0-or-1 label. Why does nobody do that?
quizzes.answer: Squared error on a sigmoid output is non-convex and its gradient vanishes exactly where the model is most confidently wrong

quizzes.question: What optimization advantage does binary cross-entropy have over squared error for a linear logistic model?
quizzes.answer: It is convex in the linear model coefficients, whereas squared error composed with a sigmoid need not be convex
quizzes.explanation: Convexity rules out suboptimal local minima, but does not guarantee a unique finite minimizer or convergence for every optimizer setting. Perfectly separable data can make unregularized coefficients grow without bound. A neural network using cross-entropy is generally not convex in its weights.

quizzes.question: Which of the following are formal assumptions of the classical linear regression model required for OLS to be BLUE (Best Linear Unbiased Estimator)? (Select all that apply)
quizzes.answer: The conditional mean is linear in the coefficients, with zero conditional mean error; The error variance is constant across all observations (homoscedasticity); The errors are uncorrelated across observations
quizzes.explanation: Gauss–Markov requires a correctly specified linear mean, zero conditional mean errors, full column rank, and uncorrelated errors with constant variance. Normality is not required for BLUE; it supports exact finite-sample t and F inference.

quizzes.question: Given the following summary statistics — x̄ = 5, ȳ = 10, Σ(xᵢ − x̄)(yᵢ − ȳ) = 40, Σ(xᵢ − x̄)² = 8 — what are the OLS slope β₁ and intercept β₀?
The normal equation for OLS is θ = (XᵀX)⁻¹Xᵀy. When should you prefer gradient descent over the normal equation?
quizzes.answer: When p is very large (tens of thousands or more), because inverting XᵀX is O(p³) and becomes computationally prohibitive

quizzes.question: A model achieves R² = 0.91 on the training set and R² = 0.43 on the test set. What is the most likely diagnosis?
quizzes.answer: The model is overfitting — it has learned noise in the training data and does not generalise

quizzes.question: Which of the following correctly describe the sigmoid function σ(z) = 1 / (1 + e⁻ᶻ) and its role in logistic regression? (Select all that apply)
quizzes.answer: σ(z) maps any real-valued input to the range (0, 1), making it interpretable as a probability; σ(0) = 0.5, so the decision boundary is where the linear combination of inputs equals zero; Computing σ(2) gives approximately 0.880; The sigmoid is the inverse of the logit (log-odds) function

quizzes.question: If the predicted probability P(y = 1 | x) = 0.75, what is the log-odds (logit) value?
In logistic regression, what does the negative log-likelihood loss equal when written in closed form for binary labels?
quizzes.answer: Binary cross-entropy: −[y log(p) + (1 − y) log(1 − p)], summed over all observations

quizzes.question: How do L1 and L2 regularisation differ in logistic regression? (Select all that apply)
quizzes.answer: L1 (Lasso) adds a penalty proportional to |β|, encouraging sparse solutions where some coefficients are exactly zero; L2 (Ridge) adds a penalty proportional to β², shrinking all coefficients toward zero but rarely to exactly zero; L2 regularisation is equivalent to placing a Gaussian prior on the coefficients in a Bayesian interpretation; L1 regularisation is equivalent to placing a Laplace prior on the coefficients

quizzes.question: What does the ROC curve plot, and what does an AUC of 0.5 indicate?
quizzes.answer: True Positive Rate vs False Positive Rate at each decision threshold; AUC = 0.5 means the classifier performs no better than random guessing

quizzes.question: Which of the following statements about the Gauss-Markov theorem are correct? (Select all that apply)
quizzes.answer: It states that OLS is the Best Linear Unbiased Estimator (BLUE) under the classical assumptions; BLUE means OLS has the smallest variance among all linear unbiased estimators; If homoscedasticity is violated, OLS is no longer BLUE — Weighted Least Squares may be more efficient

quizzes.question: Newton's method updates model parameters using the gradient and the Hessian. Compared to gradient descent, Newton's method in logistic regression typically:
quizzes.answer: Converges in far fewer iterations because it uses second-order curvature information, but each step is more expensive to compute

quizzes.question: A logistic regression model achieves 95% accuracy on a dataset where 95% of examples belong to class 0. What is the correct interpretation?
quizzes.answer: Accuracy is misleading here: a trivial classifier that always predicts class 0 would also achieve 95% accuracy. Metrics like AUC, precision, and recall are more informative for imbalanced classes

quizzes.question: Which of the following are differences between linear and logistic regression? (Select all that apply)
quizzes.answer: Linear regression predicts a continuous response; logistic regression predicts a probability for a categorical outcome; Logistic regression applies the sigmoid function to the linear combination of inputs to bound the output between 0 and 1; Linear regression can be solved with a closed-form normal equation; logistic regression has no closed-form solution and requires iterative optimisation

headings.text: Module 1: Decision Trees — Intuition and Structure

quizzes.question: A loan application arrives. The tree asks about income, then about employment, and reaches a decision. It never asked about credit score, which is also a column in the data. Is that a bug?
quizzes.answer: No — a tree follows one path, so any feature not on that path plays no part in that particular prediction

quizzes.question: Each test in a tree compares one feature against one threshold. What shape can the resulting decision boundary have?
quizzes.answer: Only rectangles — every boundary segment is parallel to a feature axis

quizzes.question: A decision tree predicts using the leaf a sample reaches during traversal. For a classification tree, what value does a leaf store?
quizzes.answer: The majority class among training samples that fell into that leaf

headings.text: Module 2: Impurity Measures and the Training Process

quizzes.question: A node contains 50 approvals and 50 rejections. Another contains 100 approvals and nothing else. Which one should an impurity measure score as zero?
quizzes.answer: The pure one, since there is nothing left to separate

quizzes.question: A split sends 90 samples into one child and 10 into the other. When you measure how good the split was, should both children count equally?
quizzes.answer: No — weight each child by how many samples it holds, or a tiny pure child would flatter a bad split

quizzes.question: Gini and entropy are different formulas. In practice, how often do they choose different splits?
quizzes.answer: Rarely — they agree on nearly all splits, and depth limits matter far more

quizzes.question: Which impurity measure is NOT recommended as a splitting criterion in CART because it can report zero gain even when a split clearly improves class separation?
quizzes.answer: Misclassification rate

headings.text: 3. Full Worked Example — Step by Step

quizzes.question: A continuous feature takes 1,000 distinct values in your data. How many thresholds does the algorithm actually need to test for it?
quizzes.answer: At most 999 — only the midpoints between consecutive sorted values can ever change the split

quizzes.question: A categorical feature has 20 levels. How many ways are there to divide those levels into two groups for a binary split?
quizzes.answer: Over half a million — the number of subsets grows exponentially with the number of levels

quizzes.question: Why are midpoints used as candidate split thresholds rather than the raw feature values themselves?
quizzes.answer: Any threshold in the interval (vᵢ, vᵢ₊₁) produces the same partition; the midpoint is a canonical representative

quizzes.question: You remove one training row from a dataset and retrain the tree. How different can the new tree be?
quizzes.answer: Potentially unrecognisable, because a changed root split rewrites every branch beneath it

quizzes.question: Let a tree grow with no limits until every leaf is pure. What is its accuracy on the training data, and what does that tell you about new data?
quizzes.answer: 100% on training and nothing about new data, because it has memorised individual rows

quizzes.question: Early stopping halts a split when it does not improve things enough. What can that miss?
quizzes.answer: A weak split whose children would have allowed an excellent split underneath it

quizzes.question: A decision tree achieves 100% training accuracy but 62% validation accuracy. Which limitation is most directly responsible?
quizzes.answer: The tree has overfitted — it memorized training noise rather than learning generalizable patterns

quizzes.question: You draw n samples with replacement from a dataset of n rows. Roughly what fraction of the original rows never get drawn at all?
quizzes.answer: About 37%, which is where the out-of-bag estimate comes from

quizzes.question: You bag 500 trees but one feature is so strong that nearly every tree picks it at the root. Do the 500 trees give you 500 independent opinions?
quizzes.answer: No — they are highly correlated, and averaging correlated errors removes far less variance

quizzes.question: In a random forest with p = 100 features, approximately how many features are considered at each split by default for a classification task, and why?
quizzes.answer: 10 features (√100) — to decorrelate trees by preventing the dominant feature from dominating every split

headings.text: 1. Bias vs. Variance — Two Different Problems
3. The General Framework — Functional Gradient Descent

quizzes.question: A random forest averages many deep trees fitted independently. Boosting fits trees one after another. What does each new tree in a boosting sequence actually try to predict?
quizzes.answer: The error left over by the trees already fitted

quizzes.question: Random forests use deep, fully grown trees. Boosting typically uses trees only a few levels deep. Why the difference?
quizzes.answer: Each boosting tree only needs to nudge the residual — deep trees would fit the noise in it and the sequence would overfit immediately

quizzes.question: Why can gradient boosting reduce bias while bagging cannot?
quizzes.answer: Gradient boosting trains models sequentially, where each new model corrects the errors of the previous ensemble — directly targeting and reducing systematic prediction error

quizzes.question: You have time to tune three hyperparameters properly. For gradient boosting, which pair should you never tune independently?
quizzes.answer: Learning rate and number of trees — halving the rate roughly doubles the trees you need

quizzes.question: Adding more trees to a random forest and adding more rounds to a boosting model have opposite risks. Which one can overfit from too many trees?
quizzes.answer: Boosting, because every round fits the remaining residual and eventually starts fitting noise

quizzes.question: You set learning_rate=0.05 instead of 0.1 in your gradient boosting model, keeping n_estimators the same. What will most likely happen?
quizzes.answer: The model underfits — smaller steps with the same number of iterations means the model cannot reach the same fitting level

quizzes.question: A decision tree makes predictions by routing a data point from the root node down through a series of binary tests. What does a leaf node represent?
quizzes.answer: The final predicted class label or regression value for all samples that reach it

quizzes.question: A node contains 40 samples: 25 belong to class A and 15 belong to class B. What is the Gini impurity of this node?
A node contains 30 positive and 30 negative examples. What is the entropy of this node (in bits)?
quizzes.answer: 1.0 bit

quizzes.question: A parent node has Gini impurity 0.48. After the best split, the left child has Gini 0.32 (n=20 samples) and the right child has Gini 0.25 (n=30 samples). Total samples = 50. Which of the following statements are correct? (Select all that apply.)
quizzes.answer: The weighted child Gini is (20/50) × 0.32 + (30/50) × 0.25 = 0.278; The information gain of this split is 0.48 − 0.278 = 0.202; The weighted child Gini is (20/50) × 0.32 + (30/50) × 0.25 = 0.128 + 0.150 = 0.278; CART uses this Gini-based information gain to select the best feature and threshold

quizzes.question: The CART algorithm searches for the best split on a continuous feature. What is the correct procedure for generating candidate thresholds?
quizzes.answer: Sort the unique feature values and evaluate midpoints between consecutive sorted values as candidate thresholds

quizzes.question: Which of the following are genuine advantages of decision trees over linear models? (Select all that apply.)
quizzes.answer: They can capture non-linear relationships without feature engineering; They natively handle a mix of numeric and categorical features; They are interpretable — a single tree can be visualized and explained step by step; They require no feature scaling or normalization

quizzes.question: You train a decision tree with no depth limit and observe perfect training accuracy but poor test accuracy. Which technique directly addresses this by penalizing tree complexity with a scalar α during post-training?
quizzes.answer: Cost-complexity pruning (ccp_alpha)

quizzes.question: In a Random Forest with p total features, how many features are randomly considered at each split for a classification task, and why is this beneficial?
quizzes.answer: √p features; this decorrelates the individual trees, reducing ensemble variance

quizzes.question: Which of the following correctly describe Out-of-Bag (OOB) error estimation in Random Forests? (Select all that apply.)
quizzes.answer: Each bootstrap sample leaves roughly 37 % of training points unused — these are the OOB samples for that tree; OOB error is computed by predicting each training point using only trees for which it was not in the bootstrap sample; OOB error is a free, approximately unbiased estimate of generalization error

quizzes.question: In gradient boosting, the model at step m is updated as F_m(x) = F_{m−1}(x) + η · h_m(x), where h_m is a new weak learner. What does h_m fit to?
quizzes.answer: The pseudo-residuals — the negative gradient of the loss with respect to the current model's predictions

quizzes.question: XGBoost improves on standard gradient boosting by using a second-order Taylor expansion of the loss. What is the practical benefit of this approach?
quizzes.answer: It allows exact computation of optimal leaf weights in closed form, leading to faster convergence

quizzes.question: You are tuning a gradient boosting model and want to reduce overfitting. Which hyperparameter changes move the model toward lower variance? (Select all that apply.)
quizzes.answer: Decrease max_depth; Decrease learning_rate (shrinkage); Decrease subsample (use a fraction of training rows per tree); Decrease colsample_bytree (use a fraction of features per tree)

quizzes.question: You compare two models: Model A uses `max_depth=2` and `n_estimators=500`; Model B uses `max_depth=8` and `n_estimators=50`. Assuming the same dataset and learning rate, which statement best describes the bias-variance tradeoff between them?
quizzes.answer: Model A has higher bias and lower variance; Model B has lower bias and higher variance

headings.text: Module 1: Why Clustering? Intuition and K-Means

quizzes.question: You have 300 unlabelled points and want 3 groups. You pick 3 points at random to act as group centres, then send every point to its nearest centre. What should happen next?
quizzes.answer: Move each centre to the average of the points that joined it, then re-assign everyone

quizzes.question: Each K-means iteration re-assigns points and then moves centroids. Can the total within-cluster distance ever go UP between one iteration and the next?
quizzes.answer: No — each step can only lower it or leave it unchanged, which is why the algorithm must stop

quizzes.question: Plain K-means drops all K starting centroids uniformly at random. Two of them happen to land inside the same dense blob. What goes wrong?
quizzes.answer: That blob gets split in two while a real cluster elsewhere gets no centroid, and iterating never escapes it

quizzes.question: In the K-means assignment step, each point is assigned to the cluster whose centroid minimises what quantity?
quizzes.answer: The squared Euclidean distance to the centroid

quizzes.question: A taxi in Manhattan drives from one corner to another, three blocks east and four blocks north. A helicopter flies the same trip. Do they cover the same distance?
quizzes.answer: No — the helicopter covers 5 blocks, the taxi 7

quizzes.question: K-means moves each centroid to the arithmetic mean of its points. Is that a convenient convention, or is the mean forced on us by something?
quizzes.answer: Forced: the mean is provably the unique minimiser of squared Euclidean distance

quizzes.question: Your table has age from 0 to 80 and income from 0 to 100,000, and you run K-means without scaling anything. What do the resulting clusters actually represent?
quizzes.answer: Income bands — a 60-year age gap contributes 3,600 to squared distance while a 1,000-rupee gap contributes 1,000,000

quizzes.question: Why must features be standardised before running K-means?
quizzes.answer: Features with larger numeric ranges dominate Euclidean distance, causing the algorithm to cluster by scale rather than structure

headings.text: Module 3: Inertia (WCSS) and the Elbow Method

quizzes.question: You run K-means for every K from 1 up to the number of data points and record the within-cluster sum of squares each time. What does the curve do, and what is its value at the last K?
quizzes.answer: It falls the whole way and reaches exactly zero when every point is its own cluster

quizzes.question: Below the true number of clusters, each extra cluster separates a genuinely different group. Above it, each extra cluster only splits an already-tight group. What does that do to the shape of the curve?
quizzes.answer: It bends: large drops turn into small ones, and the bend is the elbow

quizzes.question: You feed pure uniform random noise, with no cluster structure whatsoever, to the elbow method. What answer does it give?
quizzes.answer: It still produces a plausible-looking elbow and names a K

quizzes.question: Why can't WCSS alone be used to select the optimal number of clusters K?
quizzes.answer: WCSS monotonically decreases as K increases, reaching zero at K = n

quizzes.question: Two clusterings have identical within-cluster sum of squares. In one, the two clusters sit far apart. In the other, they nearly touch. Can that measure tell them apart?
quizzes.answer: No — it only measures tightness and never looks at the gap between clusters

quizzes.question: A point's average distance to its own cluster is 4. Its average distance to the nearest other cluster is 2. What should a good score say about that point?
quizzes.answer: That it is probably in the wrong cluster, and the score should go negative

quizzes.question: A data point has a(i) = 3.2 and b(i) = 1.8. What does this indicate about its cluster assignment?
quizzes.answer: The point may be misclustered — it is closer on average to a competing cluster than to its own

quizzes.question: K-means clustering is described as an unsupervised learning algorithm. What does 'unsupervised' mean in this context?
quizzes.answer: The training data has no class labels — the algorithm finds structure from the feature values alone

quizzes.question: What is the correct order of the four steps in the K-means algorithm?
quizzes.answer: Initialize centroids → assign each point to its nearest centroid → update centroids to the mean of their cluster → repeat until convergence

quizzes.question: Point A = (1, 2) and Point B = (4, 6). What are the Euclidean and Manhattan distances between A and B?
quizzes.answer: Euclidean = 5, Manhattan = 7

quizzes.question: Which of the following statements about distance metrics used in clustering are correct? (Select all that apply.)
quizzes.answer: Euclidean distance is computed as √(Σ(xᵢ − yᵢ)²) over all dimensions; Manhattan distance sums the absolute differences in each dimension: Σ|xᵢ − yᵢ|; Cosine similarity measures the angle between two vectors and ranges from −1 to 1; When features are on very different scales, Euclidean distance can be dominated by the largest-magnitude feature

quizzes.question: A cluster contains three points: (1, 1), (3, 1), and (2, 3). What are the coordinates of the centroid of this cluster?
After K-means converges, each point is assigned to the cluster whose centroid is closest to it. What geometric property does this create for the cluster boundaries?
quizzes.answer: Linear (straight-line) boundaries — specifically, the perpendicular bisectors between centroid pairs, forming a Voronoi diagram

quizzes.question: WCSS (Within-Cluster Sum of Squares) is defined as Σₖ Σᵢ∈Cₖ ‖xᵢ − μₖ‖². What happens to WCSS as K increases from 1 to N (number of data points)?
quizzes.answer: WCSS always decreases monotonically, reaching 0 when K = N (each point is its own cluster)

quizzes.question: Which of the following correctly describe the elbow method for choosing K? (Select all that apply.)
quizzes.answer: You plot WCSS against K and look for the point where the rate of decrease sharply slows — the 'elbow'; The elbow represents a point of diminishing returns: adding more clusters gives little benefit in compactness; K = 1 gives the maximum possible WCSS because all points are measured against a single global centroid; The method can be used alongside the silhouette score to validate the chosen K

quizzes.question: Point p has an average intra-cluster distance a(p) = 2.0 and an average distance to the nearest other cluster b(p) = 5.0. What is the silhouette score s(p)?
Which of the following statements about the silhouette score are correct? (Select all that apply.)
quizzes.answer: s(i) = (b(i) − a(i)) / max(a(i), b(i)); A score close to +1 means the point is well-matched to its own cluster and poorly matched to neighboring clusters; A score close to 0 means the point is near the boundary between two clusters; A score close to −1 means the point is probably assigned to the wrong cluster

quizzes.question: You run K-means five times with random initialization and get noticeably different final WCSS values each time. What is the most likely cause, and what is the standard remedy?
quizzes.answer: K-means converges to different local minima depending on the initial centroid placement; remedy is to run multiple restarts and keep the result with the lowest WCSS, or use K-means++ initialization

quizzes.question: A data scientist is comparing K-means clustering results for K=3 and K=5 on the same dataset. Which evaluation approaches are valid for choosing between them without using class labels? (Select all that apply.)
quizzes.answer: Compare the WCSS values — but remember that K=5 will always have lower WCSS regardless of cluster quality; Compute the average silhouette score for each K and prefer the K with the higher average score; Use the elbow plot to visually assess which K sits at the point of diminishing WCSS reduction; Visualize the cluster assignments (e.g., via PCA or t-SNE) and assess whether the clusters appear cohesive and well-separated

quizzes.question: Cosine similarity between two document vectors is 0.95. What does this value indicate about the documents, and how does cosine similarity differ from Euclidean distance in this context?
quizzes.answer: The documents are very similar in direction (topic/content); cosine similarity focuses on the angle between vectors and ignores magnitude, making it length-invariant unlike Euclidean distance

quizzes.question: Splitting text on spaces seems like a complete tokeniser. What does it do with the string don't, and with U.S.A.?
quizzes.answer: Keeps them as single tokens when they should be split, and splits on the wrong things elsewhere — punctuation and contractions break the rule immediately

quizzes.question: Lower-casing every word is standard normalisation. What information does it destroy?
quizzes.answer: The distinction between a proper name and an ordinary word — Apple the company and apple the fruit become identical

quizzes.question: Edit distance between two strings could be found by trying every sequence of edits. Why does nobody do that?
quizzes.answer: The number of edit sequences grows exponentially, which is why the problem is solved by dynamic programming over a grid instead

quizzes.question: What is the edit distance between 'cat' and 'car'?
A stemmer reduces running to run. What does it do with the word better?
quizzes.answer: Leaves it as better — a stemmer chops suffixes and has no dictionary to know that better relates to good

quizzes.question: A lemmatiser is given the word saw. Should it return see or saw?
quizzes.answer: It depends on the part of speech — the noun saw is a tool, the verb saw is the past of see

quizzes.question: A Porter stemmer produces 'univers' for both 'university' and 'universal'. What error type is this, and which metric does it harm?
quizzes.answer: Over-stemming — damages precision because semantically distinct words are collapsed to the same stem

quizzes.answer: Both readings are grammatical, which is why tagging needs context and statistics rather than a lookup table

quizzes.question: An HMM POS tagger learns that P(VBD | NN) is high and P(DT | DT) is near zero. What linguistic knowledge do these probabilities encode?
quizzes.answer: Transition probabilities — implicit grammar rules learned from tag bigram counts in the training corpus

quizzes.question: I saw the man with the telescope. Who has the telescope?
quizzes.answer: Undecidable from the grammar — both parse trees are valid, which is what structural ambiguity means

quizzes.question: Sentence: 'I shot an elephant in my pajamas.' Which type of ambiguity does this exhibit, and which grammar element causes it?
quizzes.answer: Structural ambiguity — PP "in my pajamas" can attach to NP "an elephant" or VP "shot", giving two valid parse trees

quizzes.question: To decide which sense of bass a sentence uses, the simplest method compares the sentence's words against each sense's dictionary definition. What does it pick?
quizzes.answer: The sense whose definition shares the most words with the surrounding context

quizzes.question: The Lesk algorithm selects the sense of a word by finding the synset whose gloss has the maximum overlap with the sentence context. 'He opened an account at the bank.' Which synset would it prefer, and why?
quizzes.answer: bank.n.01 (financial institution) — because context words like "account" appear in its gloss about deposits and financial services

quizzes.question: Raw co-occurrence counts rank the with almost every word as a top associate. What is wrong with using counts directly?
quizzes.answer: A frequent word co-occurs with everything, so the count measures its frequency rather than any specific association

quizzes.question: PMI('ice', 'the') ≈ 0 even though they co-occur millions of times in a large corpus. Why?
quizzes.answer: Because 'the' appears near virtually every word — P('the') is high enough that P('ice','the') ≈ P('ice')·P('the'), making the ratio ≈ 1 and log₂(1) = 0

quizzes.answer: Where one entity ends and the next begins — two adjacent cities would be indistinguishable from one three-word city

quizzes.question: A classifier that tags each token independently might output an inside tag with no preceding beginning tag. Why can a sequence model avoid that?
quizzes.answer: It scores whole label sequences, so it can learn that an impossible transition should never occur

quizzes.question: In BIO tagging, why is an 'I-PERSON' tag after an 'O' tag invalid, and which model enforces this constraint during decoding?
quizzes.answer: It is invalid because an inside tag without a preceding begin tag cannot form a valid entity span; a CRF enforces valid transitions by learning very negative weights for (O → I-*) transitions

quizzes.question: The dog bit the man and the man bit the dog produce identical bag-of-words vectors. Is that acceptable?
quizzes.answer: Often yes — for topic classification the words carry the signal, and the cost only bites when order is the point

quizzes.question: A word appears in every document in your corpus. What weight should it get?
quizzes.answer: Near zero — a word that appears everywhere cannot distinguish one document from another

quizzes.question: A document about quantum physics contains the word 'the' 50 times and 'entanglement' 3 times. Which word gets a higher TF-IDF score, and why?
quizzes.answer: "entanglement" — it appears frequently in this document (high TF) but rarely in other documents (high IDF), so their product is larger

quizzes.answer: Exactly zero — every one-hot vector is orthogonal to every other, so no two words are related at all

quizzes.question: Word2Vec is trained to predict context words from a target word. Once training finishes, what part of it do you keep?
quizzes.answer: The weight matrix — the prediction task was only a pretext for learning good vectors

quizzes.question: Why does negative sampling make Word2Vec training feasible despite a 50,000-word vocabulary?
quizzes.answer: It replaces the O(|V|) softmax computation with O(k) binary classifications per training step, where k = 5–20 negative samples

quizzes.question: A test sentence contains a word pair that never appeared in training. What probability does an unsmoothed model give the whole sentence?
quizzes.answer: Exactly zero, which makes the model claim a perfectly ordinary sentence is impossible

quizzes.question: A model has a perplexity of 100 on your test set. What does that number mean concretely?
quizzes.answer: At each position it was as uncertain as if choosing uniformly among 100 words

quizzes.question: A bigram language model assigns probability 0 to the sentence 'I dislike cats' because 'dislike' was never seen in training. What smoothing technique should you apply, and what does it do?
quizzes.answer: Laplace (Add-1) smoothing — it adds 1 to every bigram count, ensuring no zero probabilities, at the cost of redistributing some probability mass from seen to unseen bigrams

quizzes.question: You want to correct the spelling of the word 'recieve'. Using the noisy channel model, which expression correctly ranks candidate corrections?
quizzes.answer: argmax_w P(e|w) × P(w) — maximise the product of the channel (error) model and the language model prior

quizzes.question: Compute the Levenshtein edit distance between 'kitten' and 'sitting'. Which sequence of edits achieves the minimum cost, assuming each insertion, deletion, and substitution costs 1?
quizzes.answer: 3 edits: substitute k→s, substitute e→i, insert g at the end

quizzes.question: Which of the following statements correctly distinguish stemming from lemmatisation? (Select all that apply.)
quizzes.answer: Stemming strips affixes heuristically and may produce non-words (e.g. 'studies' → 'studi'); Lemmatisation returns the canonical dictionary form (lemma), so 'better' → 'good'; Stemming is generally faster than lemmatisation because it requires no vocabulary lookup

quizzes.question: In Penn Treebank POS tagging, the tag sequence for the phrase 'The old dog barked loudly' is most likely:
quizzes.answer: DT JJ NN VBD RB

quizzes.answer: One parse attaches 'with the telescope' to the VP, meaning the subject used a telescope to see; One parse attaches 'with the telescope' to the NP 'the man', meaning the man had the telescope; The CYK algorithm can detect and enumerate both parses in O(n³ |G|) time

quizzes.question: In WordNet, 'poodle' is a hyponym of 'dog', and 'dog' is a hyponym of 'animal'. What does this relationship imply about their synsets?
quizzes.answer: 'Poodle' inherits all properties of 'dog', which inherits all properties of 'animal' — hypernymy forms an IS-A hierarchy

quizzes.question: PMI is computed as log[P(w,c) / (P(w) × P(c))]. Given P(w) = 0.01, P(c) = 0.02, and P(w,c) = 0.004, compute PMI using natural logarithm (round to 2 decimal places).

quizzes.answer: 'Apple' → B-ORG, 'Inc.' → I-ORG; 'Tim' → B-PER, 'Cook' → I-PER; 'Cupertino' → B-LOC

quizzes.question: In the skip-gram variant of word2vec, what is the training objective?
quizzes.answer: Predict each context word in a surrounding window given the centre word

quizzes.question: A Viterbi decoder for POS tagging fills a trellis left-to-right. At each cell (tag t, position i) it stores the maximum probability path ending with tag t at position i. Which two quantities does it combine at each step?
quizzes.answer: The emission probability P(word_i | tag t) and the transition probability P(tag t | tag t-1) of the most probable previous tag

quizzes.question: Which of the following are true properties of PPMI (Positive PMI) compared to raw PMI? (Select all that apply.)
quizzes.answer: PPMI replaces all negative PMI values with 0, removing the bias against rare co-occurrences; PPMI retains large positive values, which indicate words that co-occur more often than chance; PPMI is preferred over raw PMI for building distributional word vectors because negative PMI values are unreliable estimates for rare events

quizzes.question: A bigram language model trained on a small corpus assigns zero probability to the test sentence 'cats eat sushi' because the bigram ('eat', 'sushi') was never observed. After applying Laplace (Add-1) smoothing with vocabulary size |V| = 500, which formula correctly gives the smoothed probability P(sushi | eat)?
quizzes.answer: P(sushi | eat) = (C(eat, sushi) + 1) / (C(eat) + 500)

quizzes.answer: No — no straight line exists, which is the fact that stalled the field for a decade

quizzes.question: You stack three linear layers with no activation between them. How expressive is the result compared to one linear layer?
quizzes.answer: Exactly as expressive — the composition of linear maps is a single linear map

quizzes.question: The universal approximation theorem says one hidden layer can approximate any continuous function. So why build deep networks?
quizzes.answer: Because it says nothing about how wide that layer must be — depth reaches the same functions with exponentially fewer units

quizzes.question: Why can't a network without nonlinear activation functions benefit from additional hidden layers?
quizzes.answer: Because linear transformations composed together are still a single linear transformation

quizzes.question: Which statements about the Universal Approximation Theorem are correct?
quizzes.answer: A single hidden layer with enough neurons can approximate any continuous function; Deeper networks are generally more parameter-efficient than wider shallow networks; Nonlinear activations are required for the theorem to hold

quizzes.question: You add a tensor of shape (32, 10) to one of shape (10,). Does that fail?
quizzes.answer: No — broadcasting stretches the smaller one across the batch dimension, which is how a bias vector is added

quizzes.question: What does torch.mm(A, B) require about its inputs?
quizzes.answer: A must have shape [m, k] and B must have shape [k, n] for some k

quizzes.question: Which of the following statements about PyTorch tensors are correct?
quizzes.answer: Operations ending in _ are in-place and modify the tensor; torch.randn creates values sampled from the standard normal distribution; The @ operator performs matrix multiplication for 2-D tensors

quizzes.question: You assign a plain tensor to a module attribute and expect it to be trained. What happens?
quizzes.answer: Nothing — it is never registered, so the optimiser never sees it and the model silently learns less than you think

quizzes.question: What is the correct signature for __getitem__ in a PyTorch Dataset?
quizzes.answer: def __getitem__(self, idx): return one_sample

quizzes.question: Which of the following are true about nn.Parameter vs register_buffer?
quizzes.answer: nn.Parameter tensors are updated by the optimizer during training; Buffers are saved in the model's state_dict; nn.Parameter automatically sets requires_grad=True

quizzes.question: Forward propagation stores every layer's intermediate activation. That costs memory proportional to the batch size and depth. Why not discard them?
quizzes.answer: The backward pass needs them — each layer's gradient depends on the input that layer saw

quizzes.question: Why should you use torch.no_grad() during inference?
quizzes.answer: To skip building the autograd graph, saving memory and computation

quizzes.question: Which of the following are true about forward propagation shapes in PyTorch's batch-first convention?
quizzes.answer: Input X has shape [batch_size, n_features]; nn.Linear(in, out) weight has shape [out, in]; Z and A at each layer have shape [batch_size, n_layer]; The bias vector is automatically broadcast over the batch dimension

quizzes.question: You could compute each weight's gradient independently by applying the chain rule from the loss down to it. Why does backpropagation go backwards instead?
quizzes.answer: Going backwards reuses the shared factors — computing each weight separately would repeat the same products millions of times

quizzes.question: For binary cross-entropy loss with sigmoid output, what is the output layer error signal δ[L]?
quizzes.answer: ∂L/∂z[L] = ŷ - y

quizzes.question: Which of the following are true about backpropagation?
quizzes.answer: It applies the chain rule recursively from output to input; The cached Z[l] and A[l] values from the forward pass are used during backprop; PyTorch accumulates gradients by default, requiring zero_grad() before each backward; The gradient of CE+softmax at the output is ŷ − y

quizzes.question: A sigmoid's derivative peaks at 0.25 and shrinks towards zero as its input grows. Backpropagation multiplies one such factor per layer. What happens in a 30-layer network?
quizzes.answer: The product collapses towards zero, so the earliest layers receive essentially no gradient

quizzes.question: A rectified unit outputs zero for all negative inputs, and its gradient there is zero too. What can go wrong with a unit that ends up always negative?
quizzes.answer: It can never recover — with no gradient it is never updated, which is the dying unit problem

quizzes.question: What is the maximum value of the sigmoid derivative σ'(z) at any z?
Which of the following are limitations of the ReLU activation function?
quizzes.answer: Its derivative is 0 for z ≤ 0, causing dying neurons; It is not zero-centered (always non-negative output); It can have unbounded output for large positive z

quizzes.question: Plain gradient descent uses one learning rate for every parameter. What does Adam do differently?
quizzes.answer: It keeps a per-parameter running estimate of gradient scale, so rarely updated parameters get effectively larger steps

quizzes.question: What is the main advantage of Adam over plain SGD?
quizzes.answer: Adam adapts the learning rate per-parameter using gradient history

quizzes.question: Which of the following are true about PyTorch's CrossEntropyLoss?
quizzes.answer: It expects raw logits (not softmax probabilities) as input; It expects integer class labels (not one-hot vectors); It combines log-softmax and NLLLoss in a numerically stable form

headings.text: The Problem: Vanishing and Exploding Gradients

quizzes.question: You initialise every weight in the network to zero. What happens during training?
quizzes.answer: Every unit in a layer computes the same thing and receives the same gradient forever — the network never breaks symmetry

quizzes.question: Initialisation schemes scale the random weights by the number of inputs to a unit. Why does the fan-in appear in the formula?
quizzes.answer: A unit sums many inputs, so its output variance grows with the count — dividing by it keeps activations from exploding or vanishing through depth

quizzes.question: Why must weight initialization break symmetry (not use all zeros)?
quizzes.answer: All neurons compute the same gradient, so they update identically and remain identical

quizzes.question: Which initialization strategies are correctly matched to their target activation?
quizzes.answer: Xavier/Glorot — designed for tanh and sigmoid activations; He/Kaiming — designed for ReLU, uses 2/n_in; All-zeros — valid for biases but not weights; He init sets variance to 2/n_in to compensate for ReLU zeroing half its inputs

quizzes.question: Dropout switches off a random subset of units during training. At inference time, should it keep doing that?
quizzes.answer: No — it is switched off at inference, and the activations are scaled so the expected output matches training

quizzes.question: What is the key difference between L1 and L2 regularization in terms of their effect on weights?
quizzes.answer: L2 shrinks all weights proportionally; L1 pushes some weights to exactly zero (sparsity)

quizzes.question: Which of the following are true about Batch Normalization?
quizzes.answer: It normalizes activations over the batch dimension per feature; It uses learned parameters γ (scale) and β (shift); It stores running mean and variance for inference as buffers; LayerNorm is preferred over BatchNorm for transformer models

quizzes.question: Training loss is still falling steadily while validation loss has been rising for ten epochs. What is happening?
quizzes.answer: It is memorising the training set — the gap between the curves is overfitting in progress

quizzes.question: Augmentation creates new training images by rotating and flipping existing ones. Should the same augmentations be applied to the validation set?
quizzes.answer: No — validation must measure performance on the real distribution, not a distorted one

quizzes.question: What does early stopping prevent, and how does it work?
quizzes.answer: It prevents overfitting by halting training when validation loss stops improving

quizzes.question: Which of the following best practices are recommended in a production PyTorch training loop?
quizzes.answer: Call model.train() before training epochs and model.eval() before validation; Use torch.no_grad() during validation to skip graph building; Call optimizer.zero_grad() before every loss.backward(); Use CrossEntropyLoss with logits directly rather than softmax + NLLLoss

quizzes.question: A single perceptron with two inputs computes f(x) = step(w₁x₁ + w₂x₂ + b). Why can a perceptron not learn the XOR function, regardless of the weights chosen?

quizzes.question: A 3-layer MLP has input dimension 784, hidden layer 1 of size 256, hidden layer 2 of size 128, and output layer of size 10. Counting all weight matrices and bias vectors, how many total trainable parameters does this network have?

quizzes.question: Which of the following are correct statements about PyTorch's DataLoader and Dataset abstractions? (Select all that apply.)

quizzes.question: During forward propagation through a layer z = Wx + b followed by a = ReLU(z), which values must be cached to make backpropagation efficient?
quizzes.answer: The pre-activation z (or equivalently the input x and parameters W, b), so that gradients through ReLU and the linear layer can be computed without re-running the forward pass

quizzes.question: In backpropagation, the gradient of the loss L with respect to the weight matrix W in a linear layer z = Wx is given by ∂L/∂W = δxᵀ, where δ = ∂L/∂z. If δ has shape (128,) and x has shape (256,), what is the shape of ∂L/∂W, and why must it match the shape of W?
quizzes.answer: Shape (128, 256) — δ is a column vector and xᵀ is a row vector; their outer product is (128, 256), which matches W's shape (128, 256)

quizzes.question: Which of the following correctly describe the vanishing gradient problem and strategies to address it? (Select all that apply.)
quizzes.answer: Sigmoid and tanh activation functions saturate for large input magnitudes, producing near-zero gradients that slow learning in early layers; ReLU avoids saturation for positive inputs, which mitigates vanishing gradients, but can cause 'dying ReLU' when neurons get stuck outputting 0; Leaky ReLU addresses dying ReLU by allowing a small negative slope (e.g. 0.01) for negative inputs; Using He initialisation (Var = 2/fan_in) is specifically designed for ReLU networks to maintain signal variance across layers

quizzes.question: The Adam optimiser maintains two moving averages for each parameter. What are they, and what problem does each solve compared to vanilla SGD?
quizzes.answer: m (first moment, mean of gradients) and v (second moment, mean of squared gradients); m provides momentum to smooth updates, v adapts the learning rate per parameter so that rarely-updated parameters take larger steps

quizzes.question: For a layer with fan_in = 256 and fan_out = 128, compute the variance and standard deviation prescribed by Xavier/Glorot initialisation.
Which of the following statements about Dropout and BatchNorm are correct? (Select all that apply.)
quizzes.answer: During training, Dropout randomly zeros activations with probability p and scales surviving activations by 1/(1−p) so that the expected output magnitude is unchanged; At test time, Dropout is disabled entirely — all activations pass through without scaling; BatchNorm normalises each feature across the mini-batch to zero mean and unit variance, then applies learned scale γ and shift β parameters; L1 regularisation encourages weight sparsity by adding a penalty proportional to the absolute value of weights, while L2 (weight decay) adds a penalty proportional to the squared weights

quizzes.question: The cross-entropy loss for a single correct-class prediction is L = −log(p), where p is the predicted probability assigned to the true class. If the model outputs p = 0.6 for the true class, what is the loss (natural log, rounded to 3 decimal places)?
Which of the following are valid strategies to prevent overfitting in a deep MLP? (Select all that apply.)
quizzes.answer: Early stopping: monitor validation loss and halt training when it stops improving for a patience window of epochs; Data augmentation: apply label-preserving transformations (e.g. noise injection for tabular data) to increase effective training set size; Learning rate scheduling: reduce the learning rate when validation loss plateaus (ReduceLROnPlateau) to fine-tune the weights near convergence; Weight decay (L2 regularisation): add a penalty on large weights to the loss, discouraging the model from fitting noise

quizzes.answer: For many-to-one forecasting, we want a single summary of the full sequence — the last layer's final hidden state — not per-step predictions

quizzes.question: Which of these preprocessing steps are important when using an LSTM for time-series data?
quizzes.answer: Z-score normalisation of input features to zero mean and unit variance; Creating sliding window pairs (input window, forecast horizon) from the raw time series; Gradient clipping to prevent exploding gradients during training

headings.text: Module 14: RNNs in Language — NLP Applications

quizzes.question: A bag-of-words model compares "not bad" and "bad, not acceptable". Does it see them as similar or as different?
quizzes.answer: Similar - same words appear in both

quizzes.question: In a bidirectional LSTM tagger, can the tag for a token depend on the words that come after it?
quizzes.answer: Yes - the backward pass reads future tokens too

quizzes.question: A random language model guessing uniformly over a 10,000-word vocabulary has what perplexity?
In encoder-decoder translation, a long source sentence is compressed into one fixed-size context vector. What happens to information from the early words as the sentence gets longer?
quizzes.answer: Diluted or lost - this is the bottleneck effect

quizzes.question: In the language model, why is the input to the decoder x[:, :-1] while the target is x[:, 1:]?
quizzes.answer: The model receives the first T-1 tokens as input and must predict the last T-1 tokens, each shifted one position forward

quizzes.question: Which of these statements about using RNNs for NLP applications are correct?
quizzes.answer: Bidirectional LSTMs improve NER because each token can be labeled using both past and future context; Language models are trained to predict the next token given all previous tokens; The encoder-decoder bottleneck (single context vector) is the main reason why attention was invented; Sentiment analysis using an RNN is more robust to negation than bag-of-words because the hidden state accumulates context

quizzes.question: A vanilla RNN has input dimension d = 50, hidden dimension n = 128, and output dimension k = 5. How many total learnable parameters does it have (W_x + W_h + b + W_y + b_y)?

An LSTM has input dimension d = 100 and hidden dimension n = 256. Each of the four gates has a weight matrix for the input (n × d), a weight matrix for the hidden state (n × n), and a bias vector (n). What is the total number of parameters across all four gates?

A recurrent network's W_h matrix has a spectral radius of 0.9, and the tanh derivative is approximately 0.8 at every step. Starting from a gradient magnitude of 1.0 at the output, estimate the gradient magnitude after flowing back through T = 10 steps.
quizzes.answer: Approximately 0.037

quizzes.question: Which of the following are valid reasons why a standard MLP is a poor choice for sequence classification tasks? (Select all that apply.)
quizzes.answer: MLPs require a fixed-length input, but sequences can vary in length; MLPs treat input positions symmetrically, losing word order information; MLPs carry no state across sequence positions during a forward pass

quizzes.question: Consider the sentence pair: 'The movie was not bad' vs 'The movie was bad.' A bag-of-words model assigns them almost the same representation. What linguistic phenomenon does this failure illustrate?
quizzes.answer: Negation and local order dependence

quizzes.question: You are building a named-entity recognition (NER) system. Which RNN application pattern best describes this task?
quizzes.answer: Many-to-many (synced): each input token produces a corresponding output label

quizzes.question: Which statements correctly describe how shared weights in an RNN handle variable-length sequences? (Select all that apply.)
quizzes.answer: The same W_h and W_x matrices are applied at every timestep regardless of sequence length; Sharing weights means the total parameter count does not grow with sequence length; During backpropagation, gradients with respect to W_h accumulate contributions from all T timesteps

quizzes.question:
You see this code in a training loop:

```python
hidden = hidden.detach()
output, hidden = rnn(chunk, hidden)
```

What is the purpose of `hidden.detach()`?
quizzes.answer: It prevents gradients from flowing back through the hidden state into previous chunks (truncated BPTT)

quizzes.question: An LSTM's cell update uses addition: c_t = f_t ⊙ c_{t-1} + i_t ⊙ c̃_t. Why is this additive update important for training?
quizzes.answer: The additive path allows gradients to flow back through time without being repeatedly multiplied by a gate weight, alleviating the vanishing gradient problem

quizzes.question: Which of the following statements about `pack_padded_sequence` in PyTorch are correct? (Select all that apply.)
quizzes.answer: It packs padded sequences so the RNN skips pad tokens during computation; It requires sequences to be sorted by length in descending order (when enforce_sorted=True); The returned h_n tensor holds the correct final hidden state for each sequence, not the state at the last padded position

quizzes.question: A language model assigns the following probabilities to the correct next word at each of 3 positions: P = 0.5, 0.25, 0.125. What is the cross-entropy loss (in nats) averaged over the 3 positions? (Use ln; ln 2 ≈ 0.693)
quizzes.answer: Approximately 1.386 nats

quizzes.question: Which of the following correctly describe the difference between an LSTM and a GRU? (Select all that apply.)
quizzes.answer: An LSTM has three gates (forget, input, output); a GRU has two gates (reset, update); A GRU merges the cell state and hidden state into a single hidden state; An LSTM typically has more parameters than a GRU with the same hidden dimension

quizzes.question: When training an RNN on a time series, gradient norms occasionally spike to thousands, causing NaN losses. Which intervention directly addresses this symptom?
quizzes.answer: Calling torch.nn.utils.clip_grad_norm_(model.parameters(), max_norm=1.0) before the optimiser step

quizzes.question: A classifier labels an email as spam. A second one says it is spam with probability 0.51. Which output is more useful to the team building the inbox?
quizzes.answer: The probability, because it lets the threshold be set by what a mistake costs

quizzes.question: One model learns the boundary between spam and ham directly. Another learns what spam typically looks like and what ham typically looks like, then compares. Which one could generate a plausible fake spam email?
quizzes.answer: The one that models what each class looks like

quizzes.question: A generative classifier like Naive Bayes primarily models which quantity before applying Bayes' theorem?
quizzes.answer: The class-conditional distribution P(x | y) and the prior P(y)

headings.text: Module 2: Deriving Bayes' Theorem from Conditional Probability

quizzes.question: You can easily measure how often a spam email contains the word free. What you actually want is how often an email containing free is spam. What converts one into the other?
quizzes.answer: Bayes' theorem, which flips the condition using the base rate of spam

quizzes.question: A test detects 99% of cases of a disease affecting 1% of people, and wrongly flags 5% of healthy people. Among positive results, roughly what fraction are real cases?
quizzes.answer: About 17%, because false positives from the much larger healthy group outnumber true positives

quizzes.question: In Bayes' theorem P(A|B) = P(B|A)P(A) / P(B), what role does the denominator P(B) play?
quizzes.answer: It is a normalizing constant (the total probability of the evidence, summed over all classes)

quizzes.question: You want the probability of a whole feature vector given a class. With 20 binary features, how many distinct combinations would that table need?
quizzes.answer: Over a million, and most of them never appear in any training set

quizzes.question: The naive assumption says that once you know an email is spam, seeing the word free tells you nothing extra about whether it contains money. Is that claim true of real email?
quizzes.answer: Almost never — but the classifier usually still ranks the classes correctly

quizzes.question: What does the conditional independence assumption in Naive Bayes actually claim?
quizzes.answer: That, once the class label is known, the features carry no additional information about each other

headings.text: A Realistic Dataset: Gaussian NB on Iris

quizzes.question: Training a naive Bayes classifier involves no gradient descent and no iteration. What does fitting actually consist of?
quizzes.answer: Counting — the parameters are just frequencies read off the training data

quizzes.question: A word appears in your test document but never appeared in any training document of one class. What does that class's score become?
quizzes.answer: Exactly zero, because one zero factor wipes out the whole product

quizzes.question: In the from-scratch implementation, what specifically changes when alpha (smoothing strength) increases from 0 to 1?
quizzes.answer: Every per-feature likelihood is pulled toward a uniform distribution over that feature's possible values, softening confidence
