headings.text: Module 5: Multinomial, Bernoulli & Gaussian Naive Bayes

quizzes.question: Word counts, yes-or-no flags, and continuous measurements are very different kinds of feature. What has to change in naive Bayes to handle each?
quizzes.answer: Only the likelihood term — the prior, the independence assumption and the decision rule are identical

quizzes.question: A document mentions a word five times. Multinomial naive Bayes uses the count. What does Bernoulli use, and when does that help?
quizzes.answer: Only whether the word is present at all, which helps on short texts where repetition means little

quizzes.question: Which statements about the three Naive Bayes variants are correct? (Select all that apply.)
quizzes.answer: Multinomial NB models feature values as counts and uses word frequency as evidence; Bernoulli NB explicitly penalizes the absence of a feature, not just its presence; Gaussian NB estimates a separate mean and variance for every (class, feature) pair; Choosing the wrong variant for a given feature type can silently reduce classification accuracy

headings.text: Module 6: Numerical Stability and Log-Space Computation

quizzes.question: You multiply two thousand probabilities, each around 0.2, in ordinary floating point. What is the result?
quizzes.answer: Exactly zero — the true value is far below what a 64-bit float can represent

quizzes.question: Taking the logarithm of the score turns the product into a sum. Does that change which class wins?
quizzes.answer: No — the logarithm is strictly increasing, so it preserves the ordering exactly

quizzes.question: Why does converting Naive Bayes scores to log-space avoid underflow while producing the same predicted class?
quizzes.answer: Because log(ab) = log(a) + log(b) turns a shrinking product into a sum of moderate negative numbers, and log is monotonic so arg-max is unchanged

headings.text: Module 7: Advantages and Disadvantages of Naive Bayes

quizzes.question: You have 200 labelled emails and a vocabulary of 5,000 words. Which is more likely to work: naive Bayes or a model that learns feature interactions?
quizzes.answer: Naive Bayes, because it estimates one small distribution per feature rather than a joint over all of them

quizzes.question: Naive Bayes reports 0.999 confidence on a document. Should you trust that number as a calibrated probability?
quizzes.answer: No — treating correlated features as independent multiplies the same evidence repeatedly, so confidences are pushed towards the extremes

quizzes.question: Which of the following are genuine disadvantages of Naive Bayes? (Select all that apply.)
quizzes.answer: It cannot learn interactions between features, by construction; Its predicted probabilities are often poorly calibrated even when its predicted labels are accurate; Without smoothing, a single unseen feature value can zero out an entire class score; Gaussian NB assumes each feature is normally distributed within each class, which is often only an approximation

headings.text: Module 8: Comparison with Other Classification Models
Problem 1: Model Under a Data Constraint

quizzes.question: Naive Bayes and logistic regression fitted to the same data often reach similar accuracy on large datasets. Which one tends to win when the training set is small?
quizzes.answer: Naive Bayes, because its strong assumption acts as a constraint that is worth more than flexibility when data is scarce

quizzes.question: A problem hinges on a feature interaction: the combination of two flags matters, but neither flag matters alone. Which model can represent that, naive Bayes or a decision tree?
quizzes.answer: Only the tree — naive Bayes multiplies per-feature terms and has no way to express a combination

quizzes.question: Which statements accurately compare Naive Bayes to other classifiers? (Select all that apply.)
quizzes.answer: Naive Bayes is generative (models P(x|y) and P(y)); logistic regression is discriminative (models P(y|x) directly); Decision trees can learn feature interactions automatically; Naive Bayes structurally cannot; k-NN requires no training phase but pays a high per-prediction cost; Naive Bayes pays a small training cost but predicts very fast; SVM output requires extra calibration to become a probability, while Naive Bayes produces probabilities directly (even if poorly calibrated)

quizzes.question: A generative classifier such as Naive Bayes primarily estimates which quantities from training data, before applying Bayes' theorem?
quizzes.answer: The class-conditional distribution P(x | y) and the prior P(y)

quizzes.question: A disease has prior P(D) = 0.02. A test has P(positive | D) = 0.95 and P(positive | not D) = 0.10. A patient tests positive. What is P(D | positive)?
quizzes.answer: Approximately 0.16

quizzes.question: In Bayes' theorem P(A|B) = P(B|A)P(A) / P(B), why can the denominator P(B) be dropped when building a classification decision rule over classes y?
quizzes.answer: Because P(B) does not depend on the class being scored, so it cannot change which class has the largest posterior

quizzes.question: What does the 'naive' conditional independence assumption in Naive Bayes specifically claim?
quizzes.answer: That, given the class label, features carry no additional information about one another

quizzes.question: A training set has 8 'Yes' examples and 2 'No' examples. Within 'Yes', a feature value 'A' appears 4 times; within 'No', it appears 1 time. Using unsmoothed Naive Bayes with only this one feature, what is P(Yes) x P(A|Yes) compared to P(No) x P(A|No)?
quizzes.answer: P(Yes)P(A|Yes) = 0.8 x 0.5 = 0.4; P(No)P(A|No) = 0.2 x 0.5 = 0.1, so Yes wins

quizzes.question: Which of the following are true about the zero-frequency problem in Naive Bayes? (Select all that apply.)
quizzes.answer: It occurs when a feature value never appears with a given class in training data; Without smoothing, it forces that entire class's score to exactly zero, regardless of other features; Laplace (add-alpha) smoothing fixes it by adding a small pretend count to every category; Larger alpha values push likelihood estimates further toward a uniform distribution

quizzes.question: Which Naive Bayes variant models each feature as a count (e.g. how many times a word occurs in a document)?
quizzes.answer: Multinomial Naive Bayes

quizzes.question: Given a short document containing the word 'buy' three times, how would Bernoulli NB treat this compared to Multinomial NB?
quizzes.answer: Bernoulli NB would treat it identically to a document with just one occurrence of "buy", since it only tracks presence/absence

quizzes.question: Gaussian Naive Bayes estimates which parameters for each (class, feature) pair?
quizzes.answer: A per-class, per-feature mean and variance

quizzes.question: With 3,000 features each having a typical likelihood around 0.15, why does computing the raw product P(y) x product of P(x_i|y) directly in floating point fail in practice?
quizzes.answer: The product shrinks exponentially and underflows to exactly 0.0, destroying the ability to compare classes

quizzes.question: Which of the following are true about computing Naive Bayes scores in log-space? (Select all that apply.)
quizzes.answer: log(ab) = log(a) + log(b) turns a shrinking product into a numerically safe sum; Because log is monotonically increasing, comparing log-scores yields the same arg-max class as comparing raw scores; The logsumexp trick is used to safely normalize log-scores back into probabilities without overflow or underflow

quizzes.question: Why does Naive Bayes typically need less training data than logistic regression to reach reasonable accuracy?
quizzes.answer: Because it estimates many small, low-dimensional per-feature distributions instead of a full joint interaction structure

quizzes.question: A dataset's true label depends on a conjunction of two features (both must be true together) with no individual feature being predictive alone. Which statement is correct?
quizzes.answer: Naive Bayes cannot represent this interaction regardless of data volume, because of its independence assumption, while models like decision trees can

quizzes.question: Which of the following are genuine strengths of Naive Bayes relative to other classifiers? (Select all that apply.)
quizzes.answer: Training requires only a single counting pass with no iterative optimization; It performs well on high-dimensional sparse data such as text with large vocabularies; It is naturally suited to incremental updates as new data arrives; It needs relatively little training data to produce a stable estimate

headings.text: Two Models, Zero Training Error, One Winner
Why Training Error Cannot Select a Model
Problem 1: Diagnosing from the Error Gap

quizzes.question: Two models both achieve zero error on the training set. One is a straight line through two points, the other a wiggly curve through two hundred. Which will do better on new data?
quizzes.answer: Impossible to say from training error, which is exactly the problem

quizzes.question: You make a model more flexible. Its bias falls. What happens to its variance?
quizzes.answer: It rises — flexibility means the fit follows the particular sample it was given

quizzes.question: A model achieves 0.1% training error and 22% test error. This gap is best explained by which term in the bias-variance decomposition?
quizzes.answer: High variance, because the model has fit noise specific to the training set

quizzes.question: Which statements about bias, variance, and model complexity are correct? (Select all that apply.)
quizzes.answer: Increasing model complexity generally decreases bias and increases variance; Collecting more training data primarily reduces variance, not bias; The expected test error decomposes into bias squared, plus variance, plus irreducible noise; Training error decreases or stays flat as model complexity increases, even when the added flexibility only captures noise

quizzes.question: You tune twenty hyperparameter settings, pick the one with the best test score, and report that score as your expected performance. What is wrong?
quizzes.answer: The test set has now been used to choose a model, so its score is optimistic and no longer an honest estimate

quizzes.question: A dataset is 2% fraud. You split it randomly into five folds. What can go wrong?
quizzes.answer: A fold can end up with almost no fraud cases, making its score meaningless and unstable

quizzes.question: What is the cardinal rule governing use of the test set?
quizzes.answer: It should be touched exactly once, after all modeling decisions are finalized, to produce a final honest performance estimate

quizzes.question: Which statements about validation sets and the holdout method are correct? (Select all that apply.)
quizzes.answer: A single holdout validation score can vary noticeably depending on the random seed used for the split, especially on smaller datasets; Selecting a hyperparameter based on test-set performance corrupts the test set as an honest measure of generalization; stratify=y in train_test_split preserves each class's proportion across the train and validation splits; Small datasets make the holdout method less reliable because validation carves away scarce training data and the resulting split-based estimate is itself noisier

quizzes.question: You evaluate a model on one held-out split and get 87% accuracy. You reshuffle and split again, getting 81%. Which number should you report?
quizzes.answer: Neither alone — a single split is one noisy sample, so the average over several is the honest estimate

quizzes.question: Your dataset has ten measurements per patient. You shuffle rows and run ordinary five-fold cross-validation. What has leaked?
quizzes.answer: The same patient appears in both training and validation folds, so the model recognises the patient rather than the pattern

quizzes.question: Why is K=10 (or K=5) a more common default than Leave-One-Out, even when LOO is computationally affordable?
quizzes.answer: LOO's N training sets overlap heavily and are highly correlated, so averaging them doesn't reduce variance as much as K=10's more independent folds do

quizzes.question: Which statements about K-Fold cross-validation are correct?
quizzes.answer: The final deployed model is typically retrained once on the full dataset using the hyperparameters CV validated; Increasing K generally increases the compute cost of the CV procedure; TimeSeriesSplit ensures the validation fold always comes chronologically after its paired training fold

headings.text: The Problem: Many Settings, Expensive Scoring
Random Search: Sample Instead of Enumerate
Bayesian Optimization: Learn From Past Trials

quizzes.question: You have five hyperparameters, each with five candidate values, and five-fold cross-validation. How many model fits does an exhaustive grid need?
quizzes.answer: 15,625 — the grid is the product of every axis, multiplied by the folds

quizzes.question: Of your five hyperparameters, only one really matters. A grid spends 5 distinct values on it. Random search with the same budget tries how many distinct values of it?
quizzes.answer: As many as there are trials, because every draw samples a fresh value on every axis

quizzes.question: Why does random search often find better hyperparameters than grid search for the same evaluation budget, when only a few hyperparameters actually matter?
quizzes.answer: Grid search wastes evaluations spreading evenly across unimportant axes, while random search's samples are denser and non-repeating along every individual axis, including the important ones

quizzes.question: Which statements about hyperparameter search strategies are correct?
quizzes.answer: Grid search's total cost grows multiplicatively with each additional hyperparameter added to the grid; Bayesian optimization uses the results of past evaluations to choose which setting to try next; Hyperband runs multiple successive-halving brackets with different starting budgets to hedge against picking one elimination schedule

headings.text: Why More Features Isn't Always Better
Problem 2: Filter vs. Wrapper vs. Embedded

quizzes.question: You add fifty more features to your dataset. The model has strictly more information than before. Can its test performance get worse?
quizzes.answer: Yes, because each extra dimension spreads the same data thinner and adds parameters to estimate

quizzes.question: You need to end up with fewer columns. One approach keeps a subset of the originals; the other builds new columns from combinations of them. Which keeps the result explainable to a domain expert?
quizzes.answer: Keeping a subset, because every surviving column still means what it always meant

quizzes.question: In 200 dimensions, the ratio (nearest distance) / (farthest distance) for a typical point tends to approach 1. What does this imply for distance-based methods like k-NN?
quizzes.answer: It means the notion of "nearest neighbor" stops being meaningful, since nearby and far points look almost equidistant

quizzes.question: Which statements about dimensionality and feature selection are correct? (Select all that apply.)
quizzes.answer: Covering a fixed-density grid in a d-dimensional space requires a number of points that grows exponentially with d; Adding an irrelevant feature can increase a model's variance even if that feature is never actively harmful on its own; Feature selection keeps a subset of the original, interpretable features, while dimensionality reduction creates new transformed features; Filter, wrapper, and embedded methods differ mainly in whether they use a real model's performance to score features and how much that costs

headings.text: Scoring Features One at a Time
Problem 2: Why the Interaction Gap Matters

quizzes.question: Two features are individually useless for predicting the target, but their difference predicts it perfectly. What does a filter method that scores one feature at a time do with them?
quizzes.answer: Discards both, because it never looks at two features together

quizzes.question: A feature has a perfect but U-shaped relationship with the target. What does a correlation-based filter score it?
quizzes.answer: Near zero, because correlation only detects straight-line relationships

quizzes.question: A numeric feature has a strong U-shaped (non-monotonic) relationship with a numeric target. Which filter method is most likely to correctly flag it as informative?
quizzes.answer: Mutual information, because it captures dependencies that are not linear or monotonic

quizzes.question: Which statements about filter-based feature selection are correct? (Select all that apply.)
quizzes.answer: Chi-square requires non-negative feature values, such as counts or one-hot encoded categories; Pearson correlation and the ANOVA F-test can both miss non-linear or non-monotonic relationships; Mutual information can detect arbitrary dependencies but has no simple standard significance threshold like a p-value; Filter methods score each feature independently, so they can systematically miss features that are only useful in combination with another feature

headings.text: Wrapper Methods: Let a Model Vote on Subsets
Embedded Methods: Selection Built Into Training

quizzes.question: A wrapper method evaluates subsets by actually training the model on each one. With 20 features, how many subsets exist?
quizzes.answer: Over a million, which is why wrappers use greedy stepwise search instead of an exhaustive one

quizzes.question: L1 regularisation is described as doing feature selection for free. What does it actually do to a useless feature's coefficient?
quizzes.answer: Drives it to exactly zero, which removes the feature from the model

quizzes.question: Roughly how many model fits does plain RFE (step=1, no CV) require to go from p features down to a target count k?
quizzes.answer: On the order of p - k fits, one per feature eliminated

quizzes.question: Which statements about wrapper and embedded feature selection methods are correct? (Select all that apply.)
quizzes.answer: RFECV uses cross-validation to automatically choose how many features to keep, removing the need to guess n_features_to_select; L1 (Lasso) regularization can drive coefficients to exactly zero, while L2 (Ridge) only shrinks them toward zero; A feature selected by Lasso for a linear model is not guaranteed to be the best feature for a random forest trained on the same data

headings.text: The Fix: Selection Inside the Pipeline
Nested CV: When You're Also Tuning

quizzes.question: You rank features by correlation with the target on the full dataset, keep the best fifty, then run cross-validation on those fifty. Is the resulting score honest?
quizzes.answer: No — the selection already saw the validation rows, so the score is optimistically biased

quizzes.question: You use cross-validation to pick hyperparameters and then report the best cross-validation score as your performance estimate. What is the flaw?
quizzes.answer: That score was the criterion for selection, so it is the maximum over many noisy estimates and is biased upward

quizzes.question: In the pure-noise example (1,000 random features, random binary target), why does selecting the top 20 correlated features on the full dataset before running 5-fold CV produce accuracy well above 50%?
quizzes.answer: Because with 1,000 independent random features, some will correlate with the target by pure chance, and those exact features were chosen using data that includes the later validation folds, so they appear predictive when scored on those same folds

quizzes.question: Which statements about leakage-safe feature selection are correct? (Select all that apply.)
quizzes.answer: Wrapping a selector and a model in a single Pipeline and passing that pipeline to cross_val_score refits the selector separately on each training fold; Leakage between CV training and validation folds can occur even if the true holdout test set is never touched; Tuning a hyperparameter like SelectKBest's k with GridSearchCV using the same CV folds you report as your final score is itself a (milder) form of leakage; Nested CV uses an inner CV loop for hyperparameter/feature-count selection and an outer CV loop, never used for any tuning decision, to report the final score

headings.text: Track Quiz — Model Selection & Feature Engineering
Track Quiz — Model Selection & Feature Engineering

quizzes.question: A degree-15 polynomial fit to 20 noisy training points achieves near-zero training error but performs far worse than a degree-2 polynomial on held-out data. This is a textbook case of:
quizzes.answer: Low bias, high variance (overfitting)

quizzes.question: You evaluate a model with one random train/validation split and get 91% accuracy. A colleague uses a different random seed for the same split and gets 85%. What does this gap most directly tell you?
quizzes.answer: The single holdout validation score has high variance, and one split is not a reliable estimate of generalization

quizzes.question: Why is it a mistake to repeatedly check performance on your test set while trying different hyperparameter settings, then report the best test-set score?
quizzes.answer: Every decision made based on the test score turns it into a de facto validation set, so the final reported number is no longer an honest estimate of generalization

quizzes.question: With 5-fold cross-validation on a dataset of 100 samples, how many samples are in each fold's validation set, and how many total model fits does one round of CV require?
quizzes.answer: 20 samples per fold; 5 model fits

quizzes.question: Compared to K=5, using K=10 in K-Fold CV typically:
quizzes.answer: Decreases bias in the CV estimate (larger training sets per fold, closer to using the full dataset) at the cost of more compute

quizzes.question: Why does plain (non-stratified) K-Fold CV risk misleading results on an imbalanced binary classification dataset (e.g. 95% negative, 5% positive)?
quizzes.answer: A random fold split can produce validation folds with very few or zero positive examples, making the per-fold score unstable or undefined

quizzes.question: Leave-One-Out CV (LOO) trains on N-1 samples and validates on 1, repeated N times. Despite being nearly unbiased, why can its overall CV variance still be high?
quizzes.answer: Because the N training sets overlap almost completely with each other, so the N validation scores are highly correlated rather than independent estimates

quizzes.question: You're forecasting next month's sales from a time-ordered dataset. Why is plain shuffled K-Fold CV inappropriate here, and what should you use instead?
quizzes.answer: Shuffled K-Fold can put future data in the training set while validating on the past, leaking information a real deployment would never have; use TimeSeriesSplit (expanding window) instead

quizzes.question: You have 3 hyperparameters, each with 5 candidate values, and are using 5-fold CV to score every combination. How many total model fits does an exhaustive Grid Search require?
quizzes.answer: 125 (5 x 5 x 5), each requiring 5 CV fits = 625 total, but 125 distinct hyperparameter settings

quizzes.question: Per the Bergstra & Bengio insight, why does Random Search often outperform Grid Search when only a few hyperparameters actually matter?
quizzes.answer: Grid search wastes evaluations by repeating the same values along unimportant axes, while random search never repeats a value along any single axis, so it explores the important dimensions more densely for the same budget

quizzes.question: What is the core idea behind Bayesian Optimization for hyperparameter search?
quizzes.answer: Build a probabilistic surrogate model of the score-vs-hyperparameters surface from evaluations so far, and use it to pick the next point that balances exploring uncertain regions against exploiting known-good ones

quizzes.question: In a 10-dimensional feature space, why does the notion of 'nearest neighbor' become less meaningful as dimensionality grows (the curse of dimensionality)?
quizzes.answer: As dimensions increase, the ratio of the distance to the nearest point vs. the farthest point approaches 1, so all points start looking roughly equidistant

quizzes.question: What is the key difference between feature selection and dimensionality reduction techniques like PCA?
quizzes.answer: Feature selection keeps a subset of the original, interpretable features; PCA creates new features that are linear combinations of the originals

quizzes.question: Which of the following are true about filter-based feature selection methods? (Select all that apply.)
quizzes.answer: They score each feature independently of any downstream model; Variance Threshold drops near-constant features without ever looking at the target; Mutual information can capture non-linear dependencies that Pearson correlation would miss

quizzes.question: Recursive Feature Elimination (RFE) selects features by:
quizzes.answer: Fitting a model, ranking features by the model's own importance/coefficients, dropping the weakest, and refitting — repeated until the target count is reached

quizzes.question: Why does L1 (Lasso) regularization drive some coefficients exactly to zero, while L2 (Ridge) only shrinks them toward zero without eliminating them?
quizzes.answer: The L1 penalty's constraint region has corners aligned with the coordinate axes, which the optimum is likely to land on exactly; the L2 penalty's constraint region is smooth (a sphere/ellipse) with no such corners

quizzes.question: Which of the following are genuine limitations or caveats of the methods discussed in the Wrapper & Embedded Methods module? (Select all that apply.)
quizzes.answer: Forward and backward sequential selection are greedy and are not guaranteed to find the globally optimal feature subset; Impurity-based tree feature importance is biased toward high-cardinality/continuous features; Lasso's selected features reflect a linear model's view of relevance, which may differ from what a tree-based model would find useful

quizzes.question: You rank 1,000 purely random noise features by their correlation with a random binary target, computed on the FULL dataset, then keep the top 20 and run 5-fold CV using only those 20 features. Why does this produce an artificially inflated accuracy?
quizzes.answer: The top 20 features were cherry-picked because they happened to correlate with the target, including within what are now the CV validation folds — so of course they look predictive on those same folds

quizzes.question: What does wrapping a feature selector and a classifier together in a single scikit-learn Pipeline and passing that pipeline to cross_val_score actually fix?
quizzes.answer: It ensures the entire pipeline — including feature selection — is refit from scratch on each training fold, so selection never sees that fold's validation rows

quizzes.question: Which of the following statements about leakage-safe evaluation are correct? (Select all that apply.)
quizzes.answer: Leakage can occur between CV training and validation folds, not only between train and a final held-out test set; Nested CV uses an inner CV loop for hyperparameter/feature-count selection and an outer CV loop to produce a final, unbiased score; Nested CV is generally more computationally expensive than a single CV loop because it multiplies inner and outer fold counts

quizzes.question: A bank's model refuses a loan. The applicant, by law, is entitled to a reason. The model is a 500-tree gradient boosting ensemble. Can the bank read the reason off the model?
quizzes.answer: No — five hundred interacting trees have no single readable path, which is exactly why this field exists

quizzes.question: Is the trade-off between accuracy and interpretability a law of nature?
quizzes.answer: No — on structured tabular data a well-built simple model often matches a complex one, and the trade-off is a tendency rather than a rule

quizzes.question: What core problem does Explainable AI address?
quizzes.answer: Making the decisions of accurate but opaque models understandable to humans

quizzes.question: A model reaches 99% test accuracy by keying on a watermark present only in one class. This shows that:
quizzes.answer: High accuracy can coexist with completely spurious reasoning, which only an explanation reveals

headings.text: Two Questions, Two Kinds of Answer
The Second Axis: What the Method Needs to See

quizzes.question: A model reports that income is its most important feature overall. A specific applicant was refused. Does the overall ranking explain that refusal?
quizzes.answer: Not necessarily — this applicant may have been refused for a reason that matters little on average

quizzes.question: An explanation method is described as model-agnostic. What does it require access to?
quizzes.answer: Only the ability to feed it inputs and read its outputs

quizzes.question: A model uses 'income' as its most important feature overall, but a particular applicant was denied mainly because of their debt ratio. Which explanation type captures this?
quizzes.answer: Local — it explains this single prediction

quizzes.question: What defines a model-agnostic explanation method?
quizzes.answer: It needs only the ability to query predictions, treating the model as a black box

quizzes.question: A decision boundary is wildly curved across the whole feature space. Zoom in far enough around one single point. What does it look like there?
quizzes.answer: Very nearly straight — which is what lets a simple linear model describe one prediction

quizzes.question: LIME fits a linear model to perturbed samples around the point of interest. Should every perturbed sample count equally in that fit?
quizzes.answer: No — samples nearer the point of interest must be weighted more heavily, or the fit drifts back to being global

quizzes.question: What is the central assumption that makes LIME work?
quizzes.answer: Even a nonlinear model is approximately linear in a small neighbourhood of any single point

quizzes.question: In LIME's objective, what does the complexity term Ω(g) accomplish?
quizzes.answer: It keeps the explanation sparse and readable by penalising the number of features used

headings.text: Problem 1: Why pass training data to the explainer?

quizzes.question: LIME explains a tabular prediction by perturbing the input. How does it perturb a continuous feature such as income?
quizzes.answer: It discretises the feature into bins and samples from the training distribution, so the perturbations stay realistic

quizzes.question: You run LIME twice on the exact same prediction with the same settings. Do you get the same explanation?
quizzes.answer: Not necessarily — the perturbations are random, so the fitted explanation varies between runs

quizzes.question: On text data, how does LIME generate perturbations of an input sentence?
quizzes.answer: It randomly removes words and observes how the prediction changes

quizzes.question: What is LIME's main practical weakness?
quizzes.answer: Its random perturbations make explanations unstable across runs

headings.text: The Axioms — Why SHAP Is Special

quizzes.question: Three people together produce a result, and you must split the credit fairly. The contribution of each depends on who else is already in the group. What does a fair split require you to consider?
quizzes.answer: Every possible order of joining, averaging each person's marginal contribution across all of them

quizzes.question: Many attribution methods exist. What can Shapley values claim that the others cannot?
quizzes.answer: They are the unique method satisfying a small set of fairness axioms, so the answer is not one choice among many

quizzes.question: A feature's SHAP value is defined as its:
quizzes.answer: Average marginal contribution to the prediction over all orderings of the features

quizzes.question: Which SHAP axiom guarantees that the feature contributions sum exactly to (prediction − base value)?
quizzes.answer: Efficiency

headings.text: Tree SHAP — Exact and Fast, Trees Only

quizzes.question: Exact Shapley values average over every ordering of the features. With 20 features, how many subsets does that involve?
quizzes.answer: Over a million, which is why every practical implementation approximates

quizzes.question: Tree SHAP is both exact and fast, while Kernel SHAP is approximate and slow. Why not always use Tree SHAP?
quizzes.answer: It exploits the structure of decision trees, so it only works on tree-based models

quizzes.question: Why is Tree SHAP preferred over Kernel SHAP for XGBoost models?
quizzes.answer: It computes exact Shapley values in polynomial time by exploiting tree structure

quizzes.question: In Kernel SHAP, what is the role of the background dataset?
quizzes.answer: It supplies replacement values for "absent" features so their effect can be marginalised out

headings.text: The Property That Makes SHAP Click: Additivity
The Three Plots You'll Actually Use

quizzes.question: A model predicts 0.82 for one applicant. The average prediction across everyone is 0.30. What should the feature attributions for this applicant add up to?
quizzes.answer: 0.52, the gap between this prediction and the average

quizzes.question: A SHAP summary plot shows every feature for every sample. What do the colours along one feature's row encode?
quizzes.answer: The feature's own value, so you can see whether high values push the prediction up or down

quizzes.question: The SHAP additivity property states that a prediction equals:
quizzes.answer: The base value plus the sum of all feature SHAP values, exactly

quizzes.question: How is a global feature-importance ranking obtained from SHAP?
quizzes.answer: By averaging the absolute SHAP values of each feature across many predictions

headings.text: Module 8: SHAP in Practice — Numerical & Image
Image Data: A "Feature" Is a Region

quizzes.question: You have a trained tree ensemble on tabular data and want SHAP values. Which explainer should you reach for?
quizzes.answer: The tree-specific one — it is exact and orders of magnitude faster on this model class

quizzes.question: Explaining an image classifier one pixel at a time gives an attribution per pixel. Why is that not useful?
quizzes.answer: A single pixel means nothing on its own, so the map is noise — regions of pixels are the meaningful unit

quizzes.question: When applying SHAP to images, how are 'features' typically defined?
quizzes.answer: Groups of pixels (superpixels/regions), with absent regions replaced by a baseline

quizzes.question: After computing SHAP values with TreeExplainer, summing them and adding the base value gives:
quizzes.answer: The exact model prediction for each row

quizzes.question: A ReLU unit is saturated at zero for this input, so its gradient is exactly zero. Does that mean the feature feeding it contributed nothing to the prediction?
quizzes.answer: No — the gradient is local, and a feature can matter enormously while having zero slope right here

quizzes.question: DeepLIFT explains a prediction relative to a reference input rather than in absolute terms. Why does that fix the saturation problem?
quizzes.answer: Because it measures the finite difference from the reference, which stays informative even where the local slope is zero

quizzes.question: How does DeepLIFT avoid the saturation problem that breaks plain-gradient explanations?
quizzes.answer: It explains the difference in activation relative to a reference input, not the local gradient

quizzes.question: In DeepLIFT, the reference (baseline) input determines:
quizzes.answer: The meaning of the explanation — attributions are contributions relative to that baseline

headings.text: LIME vs. SHAP — the Core Contrast

quizzes.question: LIME and SHAP explain the same prediction of the same model and disagree about which feature mattered most. Which one is wrong?
quizzes.answer: Neither necessarily — they answer subtly different questions and are approximating different quantities

quizzes.question: You need to explain ten thousand predictions from a tree ensemble, and the explanations must be consistent enough to aggregate. LIME or SHAP?
quizzes.answer: SHAP with the tree explainer, because its attributions are exact, additive and therefore safe to aggregate

quizzes.question: For a trustworthy, reproducible per-decision explanation of an XGBoost model at scale, the best choice is:
quizzes.answer: Tree SHAP, because it is exact, deterministic, fast on trees, and consistent

quizzes.question: Which statement about LIME vs. SHAP is correct?
quizzes.answer: SHAP is grounded in game theory with exact additivity, while LIME is a faster heuristic local fit

quizzes.question: What core problem does Explainable AI address?
quizzes.answer: Making the decisions of accurate but opaque models understandable to humans

quizzes.question: A regulator requires that each individual denied applicant receives the specific reasons for their own decision. This calls for what kind of explanation?
quizzes.answer: Local — explaining each single prediction

quizzes.question: What defines a model-agnostic explanation method such as LIME or Kernel SHAP?
quizzes.answer: It needs only the ability to query predictions, treating the model as a black box

quizzes.question: What is the central assumption that makes LIME work?
quizzes.answer: Even a nonlinear model is approximately linear in a small neighbourhood of any single point

quizzes.question: In LIME's objective ξ(x) = argmin L(f, g, πₓ) + Ω(g), what does the Ω(g) term do?
quizzes.answer: Keeps the explanation sparse and readable by penalising the number of features used

quizzes.question: What is LIME's main practical weakness?
quizzes.answer: Its random perturbations can make explanations unstable across runs

quizzes.question: A feature's SHAP value is defined as its:
quizzes.answer: Average marginal contribution to the prediction over all orderings of the features

quizzes.question: A model has base value 300 and predicts 500 for an instance. SHAP values are φ_size = 130 and φ_loc = 55. By the efficiency (additivity) property, what is φ_age?
Why is Tree SHAP preferred over Kernel SHAP for an XGBoost model?
quizzes.answer: It computes exact Shapley values in polynomial time by exploiting tree structure

quizzes.question: Which of the following are true about SHAP? (Select all that apply.)
quizzes.answer: The feature contributions plus the base value reconstruct the exact prediction (additivity); It is grounded in the game-theoretic Shapley value; Its consistency property means a feature's value cannot decrease if the model relies on it more in every coalition; Kernel SHAP requires a background dataset to represent "absent" features

quizzes.question: When SHAP is applied to images, a 'feature' is typically:
quizzes.answer: A group of pixels (a region), with absent regions replaced by a baseline

quizzes.question: How does DeepLIFT avoid the saturation problem that breaks plain-gradient explanations?
quizzes.answer: It explains the difference in activation relative to a reference input, rather than the local gradient

quizzes.question: Which statements correctly contrast LIME and SHAP? (Select all that apply.)
quizzes.answer: SHAP guarantees the contributions sum exactly to the prediction; LIME only approximates it; LIME is typically faster per instance and gives a quick intuitive local read; SHAP is deterministic (given a background), while LIME can vary between runs; SHAP's consistency guarantee makes it more trustworthy for feature ranking and audits

headings.text: Module 1: Why Association Rules? Support, Confidence, Lift
Three Numbers That Define a Rule

quizzes.question: Almost every supermarket basket contains a carrier bag. So the rule saying anything at all implies a carrier bag will hold in about 95% of the baskets that contain that thing. Is that a useful discovery?
quizzes.answer: No — bags are in 95% of baskets anyway, so the rule tells you nothing you did not know

quizzes.question: Beer appears in 7 of 10 baskets and milk in 8. Five baskets contain both, so buying beer is followed by milk 71% of the time. Is that a positive association?
quizzes.answer: No — milk's own baseline is 80%, so beer buyers are actually less likely than average to buy milk

quizzes.question: A rule {A} ⇒ {B} has confidence 0.9 but lift 0.8. What does this tell you?
quizzes.answer: B is very common, so the high confidence is misleading — buying A actually makes B less likely than its baseline rate

quizzes.question: A modest shop stocks 100 products. How many distinct non-empty combinations of those products could appear in a basket?
quizzes.answer: About 10 to the power 30, which is more than any computer will ever count

quizzes.question: Cola appears in only 2 of 10 baskets, below your threshold. What can you say about cola together with milk, without counting anything?
quizzes.answer: It is also below threshold, because adding an item can only remove baskets, never add them

quizzes.question: You raise the minimum support from 1% to 5% to make the run finish faster. What have you given up?
quizzes.answer: Every genuine niche pattern living in 2% of baskets, which is often where the valuable discoveries are

quizzes.question: Apriori's pruning step discards a candidate itemset before scanning the database when…
quizzes.answer: at least one of its immediate subsets is not in the frequent set of the previous level

quizzes.question: A frequent itemset of three items can be split into an antecedent and a consequent in six different ways, giving six rules. Do those six rules have different support values?
quizzes.answer: No — all six share the itemset's support, because support does not care about the direction of the arrow

quizzes.question: Bread and milk together imply diapers with confidence 0.80 and lift 1.14. Flip the arrow so milk and diapers imply bread. Same three items. Does the verdict hold?
quizzes.answer: No — the flipped rule has lift 0.95, so it is a negative association

quizzes.question: Two rules come from the same frequent itemset: {A} ⇒ {B, C} and {A, B} ⇒ {C}. Which statement is guaranteed?
quizzes.answer: confidence({A, B} ⇒ {C}) ≥ confidence({A} ⇒ {B, C}) — a larger antecedent never lowers confidence

quizzes.question: A library's Apriori function wants your transactions as a table of true and false values, one column per product. Why not just pass the lists of items?
quizzes.answer: Counting an itemset becomes a column-wise AND over a boolean matrix, which is enormously faster than searching lists

quizzes.question: Apriori reads the entire database once per level, so finding a frequent five-item set means at least five full passes. Can the same frequent itemsets be found with only two passes?
quizzes.answer: Yes — compress the whole database into a prefix tree once, then mine the tree instead of the data

quizzes.question: What is the key advantage of FP-Growth over Apriori?
quizzes.answer: It avoids generating candidate itemsets and needs only two database scans, so it is usually faster on large dense data

quizzes.question: Association rule mining is best described as which kind of task?
quizzes.answer: Unsupervised discovery of co-occurrence patterns among items in transactions

quizzes.question: For the rule {A} ⇒ {B}, which formula gives its confidence?
quizzes.answer: support(A ∪ B) / support(A)

quizzes.question: Milk appears in 8 of 10 baskets, Diaper in 7, and both together in 6. What is the confidence of {Milk} ⇒ {Diaper}?
The rule {Beer} ⇒ {Milk} has confidence ≈ 0.71, while Milk's support is 0.80. What is the lift, and what does it mean?
quizzes.answer: lift ≈ 0.89 — beer buyers are LESS likely than average to buy milk, despite the high confidence

quizzes.question: Which statements about support, confidence, and lift are correct? (Select all that apply.)
quizzes.answer: Support measures how frequently an itemset appears across all transactions; Lift = 1 indicates the antecedent and consequent are statistically independent; Lift is symmetric: lift(A ⇒ B) equals lift(B ⇒ A); Lift < 1 means the antecedent makes the consequent less likely than its baseline rate

quizzes.question: What does the anti-monotone (downward-closure) property state?
quizzes.answer: If an itemset is infrequent, all of its supersets are also infrequent

quizzes.question: With min_support = 0.3 on the 10-basket database, Cola appears in only 2 baskets. What does Apriori do with every itemset containing Cola?
quizzes.answer: Prunes them immediately — since {Cola} is infrequent, no superset of it can be frequent, so they are never counted

quizzes.question: In Apriori candidate generation, two frequent itemsets are joined into a larger candidate only when…
quizzes.answer: they share their first k−1 items (a common prefix)

quizzes.question: Which statements about the Apriori algorithm are correct? (Select all that apply.)
quizzes.answer: It processes itemsets level by level: first 1-itemsets, then 2-itemsets, and so on; A candidate is pruned before counting if any of its subsets is not frequent; It stops when a level produces no frequent itemsets; Raising min_support generally produces fewer frequent itemsets

quizzes.question: A frequent 3-itemset {Bread, Milk, Diaper} is used to generate rules. How many candidate rules (non-empty antecedent and consequent) does it produce?
{Bread, Milk} ⇒ {Diaper} has support 0.40, support({Bread,Milk}) = 0.50, and support({Diaper}) = 0.70. What are its confidence and lift?
quizzes.answer: confidence = 0.80, lift ≈ 1.14

quizzes.question: Which statements about evaluating rules with lift, leverage, and conviction are correct? (Select all that apply.)
quizzes.answer: Leverage = support(A ∪ B) − support(A)·support(B), and equals 0 under independence; Conviction is directional, so it can distinguish A ⇒ B from B ⇒ A; Ranking rules by confidence alone tends to favor rules with very common consequents; Conviction approaches infinity for a rule that is never violated

quizzes.question: What is the main reason to prefer FP-Growth over Apriori on large, dense datasets?
quizzes.answer: FP-Growth avoids candidate generation and needs only two database scans, so it is typically much faster

headings.text: Module 1: What Is a Time Series? Components & Decomposition
The Components of a Time Series

quizzes.question: You shuffle the rows of a customer table and refit a model. Nothing changes. You shuffle the rows of a daily sales table. What happens?
quizzes.answer: The signal is destroyed, because in a time series the order is the information

quizzes.question: A shop sells 200 extra units every December, whatever the size of the business. A second shop sells 20% more every December. Which one needs a multiplicative decomposition?
quizzes.answer: The second, because its seasonal swing grows in absolute terms as the trend rises

quizzes.question: A series' seasonal swings roughly double in size whenever the trend level doubles. Which model fits, and what's a common trick to handle it with additive tools?
quizzes.answer: Multiplicative model; log-transform the series first, then decompose additively

headings.text: Before Anything Fancy: The Simple Baselines

quizzes.question: Your new forecasting model achieves a root mean squared error of 42 on daily sales. Is that good?
quizzes.answer: Unanswerable until you know what simply repeating yesterday's value would score

quizzes.question: A series has a strong weekly pattern. Would the plain naive forecast, repeating yesterday's value, or the seasonal naive forecast, repeating the value from the same day last week, do better?
quizzes.answer: The seasonal one, because the same weekday is far more similar than the adjacent day

quizzes.question: Why is a plain k-fold (shuffled) cross-validation invalid for evaluating a time-series forecaster?
quizzes.answer: It shuffles rows, so the model trains on future points and is tested on past ones — leaking information backward in time

headings.text: Module 3: Exponential Smoothing — SES, Holt, Holt-Winters
The Idea: Weight Recent Points More
How Are α, β, γ Actually Chosen?

quizzes.question: Simple exponential smoothing tracks a level and nothing else. What does its forecast look like ten steps into the future?
quizzes.answer: A flat line at the last level, because nothing in the model represents a direction

quizzes.question: The smoothing parameter alpha sits between 0 and 1. You set it to 0.95. What behaviour have you asked for?
quizzes.answer: Almost no smoothing — the forecast will chase the newest observation, noise included

quizzes.question: How should the smoothing parameters be chosen in practice?
quizzes.answer: By fitting them, minimising in-sample squared error, which is maximum likelihood under Gaussian errors

quizzes.question: A series has a clear upward trend but no repeating seasonal pattern. Which exponential smoothing variant is the right minimum fit?
quizzes.answer: Holt's Linear method

headings.text: Testing for It: The ADF Test
Autocorrelation: Measuring "How Long Is the Memory"

quizzes.question: A model learns that today's value is 0.8 times yesterday's. The series has a steady upward trend. Does that learned relationship hold across the whole series?
quizzes.answer: No — with a rising mean, the relationship fitted on early data does not describe later data

quizzes.question: The augmented Dickey-Fuller test returns a large p-value on your series. What does that mean?
quizzes.answer: You have failed to reject non-stationarity — its null hypothesis is that a unit root is present

quizzes.question: Your series has a clear upward trend. You subtract each value from the next one. What have you done to the trend?
quizzes.answer: Removed it, because a constant slope becomes a constant difference

quizzes.question: The ADF test on a series returns p = 0.01. What does that mean?
quizzes.answer: Reject H0 (unit root) — the series looks stationary

headings.text: The Other Half of the Family: MA(q)

quizzes.question: An autoregressive model predicts today from the last few days. What kind of model is that, stated in terms you already know?
quizzes.answer: An ordinary linear regression whose predictors happen to be lagged copies of the target

quizzes.question: A series is genuinely driven only by the value two steps back. The plain autocorrelation at lag 4 still comes out large. Why?
quizzes.answer: Because lag 4 correlates with lag 2, which correlates with today — the correlation is inherited, not direct

quizzes.question: You forecast 30 days ahead and draw an uncertainty band. What should that band do as the horizon grows?
quizzes.answer: Widen, because each step's uncertainty compounds onto the last

quizzes.question: Why does a prediction interval for an AR forecast widen as the horizon h increases, while a confidence interval for the mean roughly does not?
quizzes.answer: Each additional forecast step compounds new forecast-error variance (via the ψ-weights), while a CI targets a fixed quantity with no such accumulation

quizzes.question: Which statements about AR models and forecast intervals are correct? (Select all that apply.)
quizzes.answer: AR(p) requires the series to be (roughly) stationary for the fitted coefficients to be meaningful over time; The order p of an AR model is typically read off from where the PACF cuts off; A prediction interval is always at least as wide as a confidence interval for the same forecast horizon; ARIMA is just ARMA fit on a differenced series to first restore stationarity

headings.text: ARIMA(p,d,q) — Folding Differencing Into the Model
SARIMA — The Same Machinery, One Season Apart

quizzes.question: You difference a series by hand, fit a model, and produce forecasts. Those forecasts are of the differenced series. What still has to happen?
quizzes.answer: They must be cumulatively summed back to the original scale, which is the I in ARIMA

quizzes.question: Monthly data has a yearly cycle. Differencing once at lag 1 removes the trend but the December spike survives. What removes it?
quizzes.answer: Differencing at lag 12, subtracting each month from the same month a year earlier

quizzes.question: SARIMA(1,0,0)(1,0,0)₁₂ is fit to monthly data. Which lags of y appear in the expanded equation?
quizzes.answer: Lags 1, 12 and 13 — the multiplicative form generates a cross-term at lag 13

quizzes.question: A SARIMA model's residual Ljung–Box test returns p = 0.003 at lag 12. What is the right next step?
quizzes.answer: Revisit the seasonal terms — autocorrelation survives in the residuals, so the model is misspecified

quizzes.question: Which statements about the ARIMA/SARIMA family are correct? (Select all that apply.)
quizzes.answer: ARIMA(0,1,0) is the random walk, i.e. the naive forecast from Module 2; AIC may only be compared between models fit at the same d and D; The seasonal block multiplies the non-seasonal polynomials, generating cross-term lags; Seasonal differencing can remove a trend as a side effect, sometimes saving a regular difference

quizzes.question: A monthly series' seasonal spikes stay a constant absolute size no matter how high the trend climbs. Which decomposition model fits?
quizzes.answer: Additive

quizzes.question: What distinguishes 'seasonality' from 'cycle' in a time series decomposition?
quizzes.answer: Seasonality repeats at a fixed, known period; a cycle has no fixed period

quizzes.question: On a pure random-walk series, which simple baseline forecaster is optimal (lowest expected RMSE)?
quizzes.answer: Naive (last value)

quizzes.question: Which statements about evaluating time-series forecasts are correct? (Select all that apply.)
quizzes.answer: RMSE is in the same units as the original series; A chronological train/test split avoids leaking future information into training; RMSE penalizes large errors more heavily than small ones, due to squaring; Moving-average forecasts always lag behind a trending series

quizzes.question: Simple Exponential Smoothing (SES) is fit with a high α (close to 1). What happens?
quizzes.answer: The forecast closely tracks the newest observations, chasing noise

quizzes.question: A series has both a trend and fixed-period seasonality. Which exponential smoothing variant is the minimum correct fit?
quizzes.answer: Holt-Winters

quizzes.question: In practice, how are the α, β, γ parameters of Holt-Winters chosen?
quizzes.answer: Fit by minimizing in-sample squared error (equivalent to MLE under Gaussian noise), e.g. via statsmodels .fit()

quizzes.question: The ADF test returns a p-value of 0.02. What is the correct conclusion?
quizzes.answer: Reject H0 — the series looks stationary

quizzes.question: Which statements about stationarity and fixing non-stationarity are correct? (Select all that apply.)
quizzes.answer: Weak stationarity requires constant mean, constant variance, and autocovariance depending only on lag; First-differencing typically removes a linear trend; A slowly-decaying ACF is a visual sign of non-stationarity; Seasonal differencing subtracts the value from one full period ago

quizzes.question: For an AR(p) process, which tool is used to identify the order p?
quizzes.answer: The PACF, reading off where it cuts off sharply

quizzes.question: Which linear system is solved to fit an AR(p) model via Yule-Walker?
quizzes.answer: A Toeplitz system built from the sample ACF values ρ0…ρp

quizzes.question: A 95% confidence interval for the mean is [48, 52]; a 95% prediction interval for the next observation is [40, 60]. Why is the PI wider?
quizzes.answer: The PI adds the irreducible noise of an individual future draw on top of the estimation error the CI already captures

quizzes.question: Why does a prediction interval for a multi-step AR forecast widen as the horizon increases?
quizzes.answer: Forecast-error variance compounds with each additional step (via the ψ-weights of the AR process)

headings.text: Why this is not just classification
Position bias, the tax on every log

quizzes.question: A classifier scores every product for a user and you show the ten highest. What is wrong with judging that by classification accuracy?
quizzes.answer: Accuracy treats all mistakes equally, but only the order of the top few positions is ever seen by anyone

quizzes.question: Your logs show that the item at position one gets clicked far more than the item at position ten. Does that mean it is a better item?
quizzes.answer: Not necessarily — it was seen more, and the position itself drives most of the gap

quizzes.question: Your retrieval stage returns 500 candidates. You change it so that the 500 are much more precise — fewer junk items — but recall@500 drops from 0.82 to 0.74. What happens end-to-end?
quizzes.answer: End-to-end metrics get worse: 8% of the items the shopper would have wanted are now unreachable, and no ranker can recover them

quizzes.question: A user viewed an item, added it to the basket, and bought it. Should those three events count equally as evidence of interest?

quizzes.question: Why does a brand-new product get a similarity of exactly 0 to every other product under item-item CF?

quizzes.question: Your team switches from popularity-sampled to purely hard negatives mined from the catalog. Training loss drops fast; online CTR falls. Most likely cause?
quizzes.answer: Many hard negatives are false negatives — items the shopper never saw — so the model is trained that its own correct recommendations are wrong

quizzes.question: In-batch negatives are free, but need a logQ correction. Why?

quizzes.question: Which statements about the encoder-decoder bottleneck are correct?

quizzes.answer: "coffee"

quizzes.question: Which statements about the step-by-step attention pipeline are correct?

quizzes.question: Why does a plain encoder-decoder's translation quality degrade as source sentence length increases?

quizzes.question: What is the key architectural change attention makes to fix the bottleneck?
quizzes.answer: It keeps every encoder hidden state and computes a fresh, step-specific weighted combination of them at each decoder step

quizzes.question: As training proceeds toward the game's ideal fixed point — where G has learned the real data distribution exactly — what does D(x) converge to, for every input x, real or generated?

quizzes.question: Ordinary supervised training finds a minimum of one loss function. GAN training alternates gradient ascent on D and gradient descent on G against the same V(D, G). What kind of point is the training actually looking for?
quizzes.answer: A saddle point of V — a maximum along D's direction and a minimum along G's direction, simultaneously

quizzes.question: What does the optimal discriminator D*(x) equal once the generator has matched the real data distribution exactly?
quizzes.answer: 1/2 for every input, because there is no longer any statistical difference to exploit

quizzes.question: Which statements about the GAN minimax game are correct?
quizzes.answer: D is trained to maximize V(D, G); G is trained to minimize the same V(D, G); GAN training searches for a saddle point of the shared value function, not a single minimum; At the Nash equilibrium, p_g equals p_data and D(x) = 1/2 everywhere; The discriminator outputs a probability that its input came from the real data distribution

headings.text: Module 3: Training Dynamics & the Non-Saturating Loss
Vanishing gradients from an early, confident D

quizzes.question: Early in training, G produces obvious fakes, so D(G(z)) is close to 0 for almost every z. In that regime, how large is the gradient of log(1 - D(G(z))) with respect to G's parameters?
quizzes.answer: Very small — the function is nearly flat exactly where G needs gradient most

quizzes.question: Instead of minimizing log(1 - D(G(z))), Goodfellow et al.'s original paper proposes G maximize log(D(G(z))) instead — same fixed point, different early-training gradient. Which region of the curve does this rewrite move G's gradient into?
quizzes.answer: The steep region near D(G(z)) ≈ 0, where the new objective has its strongest gradient

quizzes.question: Why does the original minimax loss for G give a weak gradient early in training?
quizzes.answer: Because log(1 - D(G(z))) is nearly flat when D(G(z)) is close to 0, which is where an untrained G starts

quizzes.question: Which statements about the non-saturating GAN loss are correct?
quizzes.answer: It has G maximize log(D(G(z))) instead of minimizing log(1 - D(G(z))); It supplies a steeper, more useful gradient exactly when D(G(z)) is close to 0; It is the loss almost every practical GAN implementation actually trains G with

headings.text: When G finds one answer and stops looking
Fixing it by looking at batches, not samples

quizzes.question: Suppose the real data has four distinct clusters, and G discovers that outputs resembling just one of them reliably fool D. If G's gradient only ever rewards fooling D on the current minibatch, what's the likely outcome?
quizzes.answer: G collapses onto that one cluster and stops producing the other three, since there's no direct penalty for the missing variety

quizzes.question: If the problem is that D judges samples one at a time, what's the natural fix?
quizzes.answer: Let D look at statistics across a whole minibatch of samples at once, so it can penalize low diversity directly

quizzes.question: Why does standard per-sample discrimination fail to catch mode collapse on its own?
quizzes.answer: Because D scores each sample independently, so a collapsed generator's individually realistic outputs give it no signal about missing diversity

quizzes.question: Which statements about mode collapse and its mitigations are correct?
quizzes.answer: Mode collapse means the generator produces near-identical outputs regardless of the sampled z; A discriminator that only judges samples one at a time can be fully fooled by a collapsed generator; Minibatch discrimination gives the discriminator access to batch-level diversity statistics; Feature matching is another mitigation that targets the same root cause as minibatch discrimination

headings.text: Learn the upsampling, don't hand-pick it

quizzes.question: A generator needs to go from a small spatial tensor to a full-resolution image — the opposite of what pooling does. Why does DCGAN avoid pooling layers entirely, in both G and D, rather than just using unpooling to reverse it?
quizzes.answer: Pooling and unpooling are fixed, non-learned operations — replacing them with strided convolutions lets the network learn its own spatial resizing filters

quizzes.question: DCGAN applies BatchNorm to almost every layer of both G and D — except two specific layers: G's output layer and D's input layer. What's the shared reason for both exceptions?
quizzes.answer: Those are the layers touching the actual image pixels, and normalizing them would distort the real data distribution or the desired output range

quizzes.question: What is the shared motivation for replacing pooling with strided/transposed convolutions in DCGAN?
quizzes.answer: It replaces a fixed, non-learned resizing rule with a learned one, giving the network control over what detail is kept or synthesized

quizzes.question: Which of these are DCGAN architectural guidelines?
quizzes.answer: Replace pooling with strided (D) and transposed (G) convolutions; Remove fully-connected hidden layers, keeping dense layers only at the very first/last stage; Use ReLU throughout G and LeakyReLU throughout D; Skip BatchNorm on G's output layer and D's input layer

headings.text: A divergence that goes flat on disjoint supports
Wasserstein distance and the Lipschitz constraint
Optional depth — the two-line example that settles it

quizzes.question: Early in training — and often for a long time after — the real data and the generator's output occupy almost non-overlapping regions of image space. In that regime, what happens to the gradient the original GAN loss provides?
quizzes.answer: It can vanish or become erratic, because the underlying divergence is locally flat or undefined when the two distributions barely overlap

quizzes.question: The Wasserstein (Earth Mover's) distance measures the minimum 'cost' to move probability mass from one distribution to match the other. Unlike JS divergence, does it stay meaningful and provide gradient even when the two distributions have disjoint support?
quizzes.answer: Yes — it varies smoothly with how far apart the distributions are, even with no overlap at all

quizzes.question: Why does WGAN train a 'critic' instead of a discriminator?
quizzes.answer: Because the critic approximates the Wasserstein distance directly rather than outputting a real/fake probability, and must satisfy a Lipschitz constraint to do so validly

quizzes.question: Which statements about WGAN and WGAN-GP are correct?
quizzes.answer: Wasserstein distance can stay smooth and informative even when two distributions have disjoint support; The original GAN loss's underlying JS divergence gives little gradient when distributions barely overlap; The WGAN critic must be constrained to be 1-Lipschitz for its Wasserstein-distance approximation to be valid; WGAN-GP's gradient penalty pushes the critic's gradient norm toward 1 on interpolated real/fake points

headings.text: Both networks need the label, not just one
What the label buys you architecturally

quizzes.question: To make a GAN generate specifically the digit '7' on demand, rather than a random digit, which network needs to receive the class label y as an extra input?
quizzes.answer: Both the generator and the discriminator

quizzes.question: In practice, how is the label y typically fed into G and D — as a completely separate network path, or folded into the existing input?
quizzes.answer: y is embedded or one-hot encoded and concatenated with the existing input (z for G, x for D) before the usual layers

quizzes.question: What goes wrong in a conditional GAN if only the generator receives the class label y, and the discriminator does not?
quizzes.answer: The discriminator can only judge general realism, so G could satisfy it by generating any realistic sample regardless of the requested class

quizzes.question: Which statements about conditional GANs are correct?
quizzes.answer: The generator becomes G(z, y) and the discriminator becomes D(x, y); The label y is typically concatenated with the existing input rather than requiring a separate subnetwork; Conditioning on a whole image instead of a class label is the same underlying idea behind pix2pix-style translation

headings.text: Two coupled generators instead of one
What cycle-consistency alone does not guarantee

quizzes.question: With no paired photo of the same animal as both a horse and a zebra, how can a model learn to translate between an unpaired domain X (horses) and domain Y (zebras) at all?
quizzes.answer: Train two generators, G: X→Y and F: Y→X, and require that translating there and back returns (approximately) the original image

quizzes.question: Suppose G and F were trained with only the cycle-consistency loss, no adversarial loss (no D_X, D_Y) at all. What is the trivially optimal solution to that loss on its own?
quizzes.answer: G and F both learn the identity function — the round trip is perfect, but no image ever actually gets translated into looking like the other domain

quizzes.question: Why can't CycleGAN be trained with cycle-consistency loss alone, dropping the adversarial discriminators entirely?
quizzes.answer: Because the identity function trivially minimizes cycle-consistency loss while performing no actual translation

quizzes.question: Which statements about CycleGAN are correct?
quizzes.answer: CycleGAN requires two generators (G: X→Y and F: Y→X) and two discriminators (D_X and D_Y); The cycle-consistency loss penalizes the distance between a round-trip translation and the original image; Cycle-consistency loss alone is trivially satisfied by the identity mapping, performing no real translation; The adversarial losses on D_X and D_Y are what force each generator's output to resemble its target domain

headings.text: Module 9: Evaluating GANs — Inception Score & FID
Two metrics that disagree on purpose

quizzes.question: With no tractable p(x) for a GAN to report, what do the standard GAN evaluation metrics actually measure instead?
quizzes.answer: They run generated images through a separate, pretrained image classifier and measure properties of its predictions

quizzes.question: Inception Score rewards two things at once: each image getting a confident, low-entropy class prediction (quality), and the set of predicted classes across many images being diverse (coverage). FID instead compares the full distribution of Inception features for real vs. generated images. Which metric is more likely to miss a generator that memorized a handful of sharp, high-quality modes?
quizzes.answer: Inception Score, because its diversity term is comparatively weak next to its per-image confidence term

quizzes.question: Why can Inception Score stay respectable even when a generator has partially collapsed onto a few sharp modes?
quizzes.answer: Because IS combines per-image confidence with diversity into one score, and strong per-image confidence can offset a real loss of diversity

quizzes.question: Which statements about GAN evaluation metrics are correct?
quizzes.answer: Both Inception Score and FID reuse a pretrained ImageNet classifier rather than measuring anything from the GAN's own training loss; Higher Inception Score is better; lower FID is better; FID compares full feature distributions between real and generated images, not individual images; Neither metric is fully meaningful on data very different from natural images, since both rely on an ImageNet-trained network

quizzes.question: Early in training the discriminator is nearly perfect, so its confidence that generated samples are fake is close to certainty. What does that do to the generator's original loss?
quizzes.answer: Its gradient nearly vanishes, which is exactly why the non-saturating form is used instead

quizzes.question: In the training loop above, why is D trained on a real batch and a fake batch as two separate forward/backward passes rather than one combined batch?
quizzes.answer: Separate passes make it straightforward to track and log the real-loss and fake-loss components independently, and BatchNorm statistics stay cleaner when real and fake batches aren't mixed within one forward pass
